knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional unbiasedness relative to the algorithmic history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge 0}\) be a filtration, and let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. A stochastic gradient \(G_t\) is conditionally unbiased at \(x_t\) if \(G_t\) is integrable and \[\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=
abla f(x_t)\quad	ext{almost surely}.\] Equivalently, the noise \(\xi_t:=G_t-
abla f(x_t)\) is a martingale difference: \(\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\) almost surely. Unconditional equality \(\mathbb E[G_t]=\mathbb E[
abla f(x_t)]\) alone does not imply conditional unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic gradient is conditionally unbiased when its expected value, given all information available before sampling it, equals the true gradient at the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Information available before the stochastic gradient at iteration t is sampled.
Stochastic gradient observed at the current iterate.

children.title: Biased Stochastic Gradients
children.top_down_role: Persistent, vanishing, and algorithm-induced bias regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bias classified by its asymptotic magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_t\) be an integrable stochastic gradient sampled at an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable point \(x_t\). Its conditional bias is \[b_t:=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-\nabla f(x_t).\] The oracle is biased whenever \(b_t\ne0\) with positive probability. The bias is persistent if \(\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|b_t\|>0\) with positive probability, vanishing if \(\|b_t\|\to0\) almost surely, and summably controlled relative to stepsizes \((\alpha_t)\) if \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_t\|b_t\|<\infty\) almost surely. Bias produced by clipping, smoothing, compression, or finite inner solves is algorithm-induced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional bias is the difference between the oracle’s conditional mean and the true gradient; it may persist, vanish, or be summable after weighting by stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-\nabla f(x_t)\), with regimes determined by the asymptotic behavior of \(\|b_t\|\).

children.title: Approximate First-Order Oracle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Deterministic and stochastic approximation errors in first-order feedback.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic telescoping estimate for recursively defined proximal iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\zeta_t\in\mathbb R^n\), \(v_1\in X^\star\), and \(v_{t+1}=P_{v_t}(\zeta_t)\) for \(t=1,\ldots,N\). Then, for every \(u\in X\), \[\sum_{t=1}^N\zeta_t^\top(v_t-u)\le V(v_1,u)+\frac{1}{2\kappa}\sum_{t=1}^N\|\zeta_t\|_*^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any sequence of Bregman proximal updates, the cumulative pairing of each update vector with the current displacement from any comparison point is bounded by the initial Bregman divergence plus the accumulated squared dual norms divided by twice the strong-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u\in X:\ \sum_{t=1}^N\zeta_t^\top(v_t-u)\le V(v_1,u)+(2\kappa)^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^N\|\zeta_t\|_*^2

children.title: Deterministic Oracle Inexactness
children.top_down_role: Systematic approximation error arising from deterministic first-order feedback.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Oracle Inexactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform or point-dependent deterministic error in a dual-valued first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a normed space with dual \(\mathcal X^*\), let \(D\subseteq\mathcal X\), and let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be Fréchet differentiable at every point of \(D\). A deterministic mapping \(g:D\to\mathcal X^*\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-inexact first-order oracle on \(D\) if \[\|g(x)-Df(x)\|_*\le\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }x\in D.\] More generally, for an error envelope \(e:D\to[0,\infty)\), point-dependent inexactness means \(\|g(x)-Df(x)\|_*\le e(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). This condition is deterministic and contains no sampling or expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic inexact first-order oracle returns a dual vector whose distance from the true derivative is bounded uniformly or by a prescribed point-dependent envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a normed space with dual \(\mathcal X^*\), and \(D\subseteq\mathcal X\).
\(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable at every point of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|g(x)-Df(x)\|_*\le\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of f at x, viewed as an element of the dual space.
Dual norm on the first-order oracle space.

children.title: Stochastic Approximation Error
children.top_down_role: Random approximation effects beyond ordinary sampling noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Approximation Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional mean-square decomposition of stochastic gradient error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, and suppose that both \(G_t\) and \(
abla f(x_t)\) are square-integrable. Define \(b_t:=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-
abla f(x_t)\) and \(\zeta_t:=G_t-\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\). Then \(G_t-
abla f(x_t)=b_t+\zeta_t\), where \(\mathbb E[\zeta_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\), and \[\mathbb E[\|G_t-
abla f(x_t)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]=\|b_t\|^2+\mathbb E[\|\zeta_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t].\] Thus the conditional mean-square stochastic approximation error is the sum of squared conditional bias and conditional centered variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both the stochastic gradient and the true gradient at the random iterate are square-integrable, the conditional mean-square gradient error splits exactly into squared conditional bias and centered conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\|G_t-\nabla f(x_t)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]=\|b_t\|^2+\mathbb E[\|\zeta_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\).

children.title: Persistent Oracle Distortion
children.top_down_role: Accuracy limitations when approximation errors do not vanish.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Oracle Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonvanishing oracle error can prevent exact first-order stationarity guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and the deterministic distorted oracle \(G(x)=x+b\), where \(b
e0\). Its error is the persistent constant \(G(x)-
abla f(x)=b\). The unique oracle root is \(x=-b\), whereas the true stationary point is \(x=0\). At the oracle root, \(|
abla f(-b)|=|b|\) and \(f(-b)-f(0)=b^2/2\). This example shows that persistent oracle distortion can leave irreducible stationarity and objective errors, so exact stationarity or optimality cannot be guaranteed in general without further control of the distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant gradient distortion shifts the apparent stationary point in this quadratic example, showing that persistent distortion can prevent general exact-stationarity and exact-optimality guarantees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle root \(x=-b\) has true stationarity error \(|b|\) and objective error \(b^2/2\), demonstrating failure of general exact guarantees.

children.title: Classical Concentration Noise Pair
children.top_down_role: Classical bounded-increment and Gaussian-type concentration regimes.

children.title: Almost-Surely Bounded Noise
children.top_down_role: Noise controlled through uniform magnitude limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Surely Bounded Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditional essential bound on gradient noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_t:=G_t-\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\) be the centered oracle noise in a normed finite-dimensional space. The noise is almost surely bounded by \(B<\infty\) if \[\mathbb P\!\left(\|\xi_t\|\le B\mid\mathcal F_t\right)=1\quad\text{almost surely for every }t.\] A point-dependent version replaces \(B\) by an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable bound \(B_t\). The uniform condition implies \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^p\mid\mathcal F_t]\le B^p\) almost surely for every finite \(p\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centered oracle noise is almost surely bounded when its norm never exceeds a fixed radius, conditionally on the algorithm’s current history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\|\xi_t\|\le B\mid\mathcal F_t)=1\) almost surely for every \(t\).

children.title: Sub-Gaussian Noise
children.top_down_role: Noise with Gaussian-type concentration behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Sub-Gaussian Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional directional sub-Gaussianity for vector-valued oracle noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_t\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\). It is conditionally \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian if, almost surely, \[\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda\langle u,\xi_t\rangle)\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\exp(\lambda^2\sigma^2/2)\] for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and every unit vector \(u\in\mathbb R^d\). Consequently, each directional projection obeys \[\mathbb P(|\langle u,\xi_t\rangle|\ge r\mid\mathcal F_t)\le2\exp(-r^2/(2\sigma^2))\] for every \(r\ge0\). This definition controls all directions but does not require \(\|\xi_t\|\) to be almost surely bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector noise is conditionally sub-Gaussian when every unit-direction projection has a Gaussian-type conditional moment-generating-function and tail bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every unit-direction projection has conditional tails bounded by \(2\exp(-r^2/(2\sigma^2))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directional conditional sub-Gaussian convention and resulting two-sided tail bound are mathematically standard, but no inspectable source supports the selected vector-valued conditional formulation and parameter convention.

children.title: Concentration Gap Between Regimes
children.top_down_role: Differences in guarantees enabled by bounded versus sub-Gaussian control.

knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Gap Between Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded noise is sub-Gaussian, but sub-Gaussian noise need not be bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\mathbb E[X]=0\). If \(|X|\le B\) almost surely, then Hoeffding's lemma gives \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\le e^{\lambda^2B^2/2}\quad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R,\] so bounded centered noise is \(B\)-sub-Gaussian under this parameter convention. The converse fails: if \(X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\), then \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]=e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\), but \(\mathbb P(|X|>B)>0\) for every finite \(B\). Thus almost-sure boundedness is strictly stronger than sub-Gaussian concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded centered noise always has sub-Gaussian tails, while Gaussian noise shows that sub-Gaussian concentration does not imply an almost-sure bound.
assumptions_latex: The sub-Gaussian convention is \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2s^2/2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Almost-sure boundedness implies sub-Gaussianity, whereas the reverse implication is false.

notation.meaning: Gaussian standard deviation and sub-Gaussian scale.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hoeffding lemma and Gaussian counterexample

children.title: Sub-Exponential Noise
children.top_down_role: Intermediate light-tail regimes requiring confidence-sensitive control.

knowledge_statements.title: Sub-Exponential Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional Bernstein-type control of directional noise tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi_t\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\). It is conditionally sub-exponential with parameters \((
u,b)\) if, almost surely, \[\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda\langle u,\xi_tangle)\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\exp(\lambda^2
u^2/2)\] for every unit vector \(u\) and every \(\lambda\) satisfying \(|\lambda|<1/b\). Consequently, each projection satisfies a Bernstein-type bound \[\mathbb P(|\langle u,\xi_tangle|\ge r\mid\mathcal F_t)\le2\exp\!\left[-	frac12\min\{r^2/
u^2,r/b\}ight].\] The tail is Gaussian-like for moderate deviations and exponential for large deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sub-exponential noise has Gaussian-like moderate deviations and exponential large deviations, expressed through a conditional Bernstein moment-generating-function bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Directional conditional tails decay as \(\exp[-\tfrac12\min\{r^2/\nu^2,r/b\}]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bernstein-type formulation is plausible and internally consistent, but the precise conditional MGF domain, constants, and resulting tail parameterization require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Finite-Moment Noise Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Weak-moment regimes underlying robust stochastic optimization.

children.title: Finite-Variance Noise
children.top_down_role: Heavy-tailed feedback with a finite second moment.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Variance Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditional second-moment control of centered oracle noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_t:=G_t-\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\) be centered oracle noise in \(\mathbb R^d\). The noise has uniformly bounded conditional variance if there exists \(\sigma^2<\infty\) such that \[\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\sigma^2\quad\text{almost surely for every }t.\] A nonuniform finite-variance regime permits an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable bound \(\sigma_t^2<\infty\). Finite variance alone yields polynomial tail control through conditional Markov or Chebyshev inequalities and does not imply sub-Gaussian or sub-exponential concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-variance noise has a finite conditional second moment, uniformly or iteration-wise, but this alone does not guarantee exponential tail decay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\sigma^2<\infty\) almost surely for every \(t\).

children.title: Higher-Order Finite-Moment Noise
children.top_down_role: Feedback controlled through a specified finite moment order.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Finite-Moment Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional finite-moment control at an order strictly above two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p>2\), and let \(\xi_t:=G_t-\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\) be centered oracle noise in \(\mathbb R^d\). The noise has a uniformly bounded conditional \(p\)-th moment if there exists \(M_p<\infty\) such that \[\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^p\mid\mathcal F_t]\le M_p^p\quad\text{almost surely for every }t.\] By conditional Lyapunov monotonicity, this implies \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^q\mid\mathcal F_t]\le M_p^q\) for every \(1\le q\le p\), including finite variance. It does not, for any fixed finite \(p\), imply exponential-tail concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order finite-moment noise has a bounded conditional p-th moment for some p above two, implying all lower moments but not exponential tails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^p\mid\mathcal F_t]\le M_p^p\), hence every conditional moment of order \(q\le p\) is finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional Lyapunov implication and failure of any fixed finite moment to ensure exponential tails are standard, but the record supplies neither an inspectable citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Moment-Order Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance changes associated with the available moment order.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Order Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower moments follow from higher ones, but the converse generally fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space, if \(1\le q<p<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E|X|^p<\infty\), then \[(\mathbb E|X|^q)^{1/q}\le(\mathbb E|X|^p)^{1/p}.\] The converse fails sharply. For a symmetric random variable satisfying \(\mathbb P(|X|>x)=x^{-\alpha}\) for \(x\ge1\), one has \(\mathbb E|X|^r<\infty\) exactly when \(r<\alpha\). Hence choosing \(q<\alpha\le p\) gives a finite \(q\)-th moment but an infinite \(p\)-th moment. Noise assumptions and guarantees therefore depend essentially on the specified moment order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite higher moment controls every lower moment, but a power-law example can have a finite lower moment and an infinite higher one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite \(p\)-th moment implies finite \(q\)-th moment, while finite \(q\)-th moment does not imply finite \(p\)-th moment.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Lyapunov inequality and power-law moment criterion

children.title: Extreme-Tail Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where standard mean and variance controls cease to support classical guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Tail Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which unbiasedness or finite-variance stochastic-gradient analysis becomes undefined or inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the oracle return \(G(x,\zeta)=g(x)+\xi(x,\zeta)\). If \(\mathbb{E}[\xi(x,\zeta)]\) does not exist, then the classical unbiasedness condition \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\zeta)]=g(x)\) is undefined. If the mean exists but \(\mathbb{E}\|\xi(x,\zeta)\|^2=\infty\), then no finite constant \(\sigma^2\) can satisfy \(\mathbb{E}\|G(x,\zeta)-g(x)\|^2\leq\sigma^2\). Consequently, convergence or concentration guarantees whose hypotheses require unbiased finite-variance feedback cannot be invoked without stronger tail modeling, truncation, clipping, or robust aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical unbiased-oracle analysis fails when the noise mean is undefined, while finite-variance guarantees fail when the noise has infinite second moment.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\zeta)=g(x)+\xi(x,\zeta)\) is a stochastic first-order oracle on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\xi\) nonexistent invalidates unbiasedness; \(\mathbb{E}\|\xi\|^2=\infty\) invalidates every finite uniform variance bound.
review_flags: Authoritative source for the exact heavy-tail boundary formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical implications are coherent, but no citation is supplied for the heavy-tail oracle formulation or the stated boundary of classical guarantees.

children.title: Non-IID Oracle Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Departures from independent stationary sampling that change oracle analysis.

children.title: Contaminated-Feedback Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Feedback streams containing atypical or strategically corrupted observations.

children.title: Incidental Outliers
children.top_down_role: Atypical observations arising without strategic manipulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Incidental Outliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent, nonadaptive contamination with a fixed outlier law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incidental-outlier oracle at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) has response \(Y=(1-B)G(x,\zeta)+BZ\), where \(B\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\varepsilon)\) is independent of the clean sample \(\zeta\), the outlier \(Z\), and the algorithmic history; \(G(x,\zeta)\) follows the clean oracle law; and \(Z\sim Q\) for a fixed distribution \(Q\). Equivalently, the response law is \((1-\varepsilon)P_x+\varepsilon Q\). The contamination is incidental because neither \(B\) nor \(Q\) adapts to the current iterate or observed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidental outliers arise independently with probability epsilon from a fixed outlier distribution that does not adapt to the algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(B\), \(\zeta\), and \(Z\) are mutually independent and independent of the past.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{L}(Y\mid x)=(1-\varepsilon)P_x+\varepsilon Q\).
review_flags: A source distinguishing incidental from adaptive contamination is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise and fits the incidental-outlier leaf, but the distinction between fixed independent mixture contamination and adaptive contamination requires an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Adversarial Contamination
children.top_down_role: Observations altered or inserted by an adversarial mechanism.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent epsilon-contamination of stochastic first-order responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\) be the algorithmic history and let \(P_{x_t}\) denote the clean response law at \(x_t\). An \(\varepsilon\)-adversarially contaminated oracle returns \(Y_t\) with conditional law \(\mathcal{L}(Y_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_t)=(1-\varepsilon)P_{x_t}+\varepsilon Q_t\), where \(Q_t\) is an arbitrary probability law that may depend on \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\), \(x_t\), and the algorithm. No moment, support, or unbiasedness restriction is imposed on \(Q_t\) unless stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adversary may replace an epsilon fraction of feedback using arbitrary distributions chosen from the iterate and prior algorithmic history.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{x_t}\) is the designated clean conditional response law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{L}(Y_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_t)=(1-\varepsilon)P_{x_t}+\varepsilon Q_t\) for arbitrary history-dependent \(Q_t\).
review_flags: The chosen online conditional-contamination model needs an authoritative source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional mixture model fits the adversarial-contamination leaf, but no source establishes that this particular history-dependent epsilon-mixture is the intended convention.

children.title: Contamination-Severity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural changes as the corrupted fraction or influence increases.

knowledge_statements.title: Contamination-Severity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Severity classified relative to an estimator's finite-sample contamination breakdown point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an estimator \(T_n\) applied to \(n\) oracle responses, define its replacement breakdown fraction at a clean sample \(z_{1:n}\) by \(\varepsilon_n^*(T_n;z_{1:n})=n^{-1}\min\{m:\sup_{\widetilde z_{1:n}}\|T_n(\widetilde z_{1:n})-T_n(z_{1:n})\|=\infty\}\), where \(\widetilde z_{1:n}\) differs from \(z_{1:n}\) in at most \(m\) positions. Contamination level \(\varepsilon\) is sub-breakdown when \(\varepsilon<\varepsilon_n^*\), critical when \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_n^*\), and super-breakdown when \(\varepsilon>\varepsilon_n^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contamination is subcritical, critical, or supercritical according to whether its fraction lies below, at, or above the estimator's replacement breakdown fraction.
assumptions_latex: Contamination replaces sample positions without restricting replacement magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The severity regime is determined by comparing \(\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon_n^*(T_n;z_{1:n})\).
review_flags: A robust-statistics source for this exact finite-sample breakdown convention is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition appropriately classifies severity relative to finite-sample replacement breakdown, but the exact breakdown definition and the subcritical/critical/supercritical terminology lack a cited source.

children.title: Temporally Dependent Noise Family
children.top_down_role: Temporally dependent observations and mixing-sensitive oracle behavior.

children.title: General Dependent Noise
children.top_down_role: Temporally correlated feedback without a specialized Markov representation.

knowledge_statements.title: General Dependent Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adapted oracle noise without temporal independence or a specified Markov structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_t),\mathbb{P})\), a stochastic first-order oracle has general dependent noise when \(G_t=g(x_t)+\xi_t\), with \(x_t\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\) and \(\xi_t\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_t\), while the conditional law \(\mathcal{L}(\xi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1})\) may depend on the entire history. Temporal independence, identical distribution, martingale-difference structure, and Markov dependence are not included unless imposed as additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General dependent noise may depend on the full past and need not be independent, stationary, Markovian, or a martingale difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{L}(\xi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1})\) is unrestricted beyond separately stated integrability conditions.
review_flags: A source for the intended general-dependent-oracle convention is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits general temporally dependent noise and distinguishes it from its Markovian sibling, but the unrestricted history-dependent oracle convention has no supporting citation.

children.title: Markovian Noise
children.top_down_role: Feedback generated through an underlying Markov process.

knowledge_statements.title: Markovian Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order feedback driven by a Markov state rather than fresh independent samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z_t)_{t\geq0}\) be a Markov chain with transition kernel \(K\) and invariant distribution \(\pi\). A Markovian stochastic first-order oracle returns \(G_t=G(x_t,Z_t)\), where \(x_t\) is determined from observations through time \(t-1\). Its stationary mean field is \(g(x)=\int G(x,z)\,\pi(dz)\). Even when \(g(x)=\nabla f(x)\), the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\) generally differs from \(g(x_t)\) because the conditional law of \(Z_t\) need not equal \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Markovian feedback is generated from a Markov state; its conditional gradient can remain biased until the state distribution approaches stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\int G(x,z)\,\pi(dz)\), but generally \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\neq g(x_t)\).
review_flags: An authoritative stochastic-approximation source for this Markovian oracle model is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly separates a stationary mean field from the generally biased one-step conditional mean under Markovian sampling, but an authoritative stochastic-approximation source is required.

children.title: Mixing-Time Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Guarantee degradation associated with slow temporal mixing.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixing-Time Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance inflation caused by serial correlation in stationary oracle observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Y_t)\) be a stationary scalar process with mean \(\mu\), variance \(\gamma_0>0\), and autocorrelation \(\rho_k\). For \(\overline Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\), \[\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_n)=\frac{\gamma_0}{n}\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\rho_k\right).\] If \(\sum_{k\geq1}|\rho_k|<\infty\), the asymptotic variance factor is \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k\geq1}\rho_k\). Thus slower decay of dependence increases effective oracle variance and reduces the effective sample size to approximately \(n/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) when \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Serial correlation inflates the variance of averaged feedback by the integrated autocorrelation time, reducing its effective number of independent observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_n)\to\gamma_0\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\), with effective sample size approximately \(n/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\).
review_flags: A time-series or Markov-chain source for the variance identity and interpretation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits mixing-time sensitivity and states a standard stationary-process variance identity, but neither that identity nor the effective-sample-size interpretation has a cited source.

children.title: Drifting Oracle Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Changing objectives, noise laws, and gradient scales.

children.title: Nonstationary Objective Oracles
children.top_down_role: First-order feedback associated with a changing objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Objective Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased first-order feedback for a time-varying objective sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((f_t)_{t=1}^T\) be differentiable objectives on a common domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A nonstationary objective oracle queried at \(x_t\in X\) returns \(G_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_t]=
abla f_t(x_t)\). Objective drift may be measured by \(V_T=\sum_{t=2}^T\sup_{x\in X}\|
abla f_t(x)-
abla f_{t-1}(x)\|\). When \(V_T>0\), the feedback is not generally an unbiased oracle for any single fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstationary oracle is unbiased for the current time-indexed objective, whose gradient field may drift across rounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_t]=\nabla f_t(x_t)\), with gradient-field drift summarized by \(V_T\).
review_flags: A source for this nonstationary first-order-oracle and variation-budget convention is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition cleanly distinguishes objective drift from noise-law drift, but the time-indexed oracle and cumulative gradient-field variation convention require a source.

children.title: Drifting Noise Laws
children.top_down_role: Feedback whose stochastic distribution changes over time.

knowledge_statements.title: Drifting Noise Laws
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed mean field observed through time-varying conditional noise distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed target field \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}^d\), an oracle with drifting noise laws returns \(G_t=g(x_t)+\xi_t\), where \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0\) but \(P_t=\mathcal{L}(\xi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1})\) may vary with \(t\). Given a probability metric \(D\), its cumulative distributional drift is \(\Delta_T=\sum_{t=2}^T D(P_t,P_{t-1})\). This regime separates changing noise distributions from objective drift because the conditional mean field \(g\) remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The target gradient field stays fixed, but the conditional noise distribution changes over time and is measured by a distributional drift budget.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\xi_t\) is conditionally integrable and centered.
\(D\) is a specified metric on the relevant probability laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mean field is time invariant while \(\Delta_T=\sum_{t=2}^T D(P_t,P_{t-1})\) quantifies noise-law drift.

notation.meaning: conditional noise law at round t

review_flags: The probability metric and conditioning convention require source alignment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the drifting-noise-law leaf, but the conditional-law formulation and metric-based drift budget are convention-dependent and unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Gradient-Scale Drift
children.top_down_role: Temporal changes in the magnitude scale of observed gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Scale Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time variation in the conditional magnitude scale of stochastic first-order responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be the oracle response and define its predictable root-mean-square scale by \(s_t(x_t)=\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\|G_t\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_t]\bigr)^{1/2}\). Gradient-scale drift is present when no constant \(s\) satisfies \(s_t(x_t)=s\) for all \(t\). A finite-horizon drift budget is \(S_T=\sum_{t=2}^T|s_t(x_t)-s_{t-1}(x_{t-1})|\). Uniform bounded-scale analysis additionally requires \(\sup_{t\leq T}s_t(x_t)<\infty\); scale drift alone does not imply this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-scale drift means the conditional RMS magnitude of feedback varies over time; total variation and uniform boundedness are separate conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) has a finite conditional second moment at each round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scale drift is characterized by time variation of \(s_t(x_t)\), and its pathwise magnitude is summarized by \(S_T\).
review_flags: A source is needed to confirm RMS scale and total-variation conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition distinguishes time variation from uniform boundedness, but defining gradient scale by conditional RMS response magnitude and measuring its pathwise total variation requires source support.

children.title: Structured First-Order Feedback
children.top_down_role: First-order oracle interfaces whose detailed algorithms belong to neighboring chapters.

children.title: Composite Forward-Backward Feedback
children.top_down_role: Stochastic forward information coupled to exactly handled composite structure.

assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\)-measurable, and \(G_t\) is conditionally integrable with \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\nabla f(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta_t h}(x_t-\eta_tG_t)\), and the prescribed terminal output is \(x_T\).

notation.meaning: algorithmic history available before the round-t oracle response

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic forward step for a smooth term followed by an exact proximal backward step.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\) denote the algorithmic history available before the round-\(t\) oracle response. Given \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}h\), a horizon \(T\in\mathbb{N}\), and stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), consider minimizing \(F(x)=f(x)+h(x)\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex. At round \(t\), with \(x_t\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\), obtain an integrable response \(G_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\nabla f(x_t)\), and then update \[x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta_t h}(x_t-\eta_tG_t),\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(v)=\arg\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{h(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{2\eta}\right\}.\] After \(T\) updates, output \(x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each round, use a stochastic gradient estimate that is unbiased conditional on the history available before sampling, then apply the exact proximal map of the nonsmooth convex term.

children.title: Partitioned Feedback Granularity
children.top_down_role: Partial stochastic information aligned with coordinate or block decompositions.

children.title: Coordinate Feedback
children.top_down_role: Stochastic information restricted to individual coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feedback revealing one sampled coordinate of a first-order vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), a coordinate-feedback oracle queried at \(x\) samples \(I\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\) with probabilities \(p_i>0\) and returns \((I,Y)\), where \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x,I=i]=\partial_i f(x)\). The reconstructed estimator \(\widehat g=(Y/p_I)e_I\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\). Without the factor \(1/p_I\), the embedded response \(Ye_I\) has conditional mean \(\sum_{i=1}^d p_i\partial_i f(x)e_i\), which is generally not the full gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle reveals one sampled gradient coordinate; inverse-probability scaling reconstructs an unbiased full-gradient estimator.
assumptions_latex: The scalar coordinate response is conditionally integrable and unbiased.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[(Y/p_I)e_I\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).

source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals
source_refs.locator: One Coordinate at a Time p. 56

review_flags: The locator may cover coordinate updates rather than the stochastic inverse-probability feedback formulation.

source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals
source_witnesses.locator: One Coordinate at a Time p. 56

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and inverse-probability calculation are mathematically coherent and fit coordinate feedback, but the cited locator appears to concern coordinate-wise updates and may not support the stochastic coordinate oracle or inverse-probability reconstruction. A directly supporting source is required.

children.title: Block Feedback
children.top_down_role: Stochastic information exposed through grouped variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stochastic first-order feedback restricted to one block of a fixed product decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb{R}^d=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\), with block projections \(P_i\), and let \(G(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be a stochastic first-order oracle. Given a sampled block \(I\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), block feedback at \(x\) is \(Y=P_I G(x,\xi)\), together with the identity of \(I\). If \(I\) is independent of \(\xi\), has probabilities \(p_i>0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\), then the importance-corrected estimator \(\widehat G=p_I^{-1}P_I G(x,\xi)\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat G\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block feedback reveals only a sampled block of a stochastic gradient; inverse-probability scaling restores unbiased full-gradient estimation when every block has positive sampling probability.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is independent of \(\xi\) conditionally on \(x\), and \(p_i=\mathbb{P}(I=i\mid x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[p_I^{-1}P_I G(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Conditional probability of sampling block i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and importance-correction identity fit the Block Feedback leaf and are mathematically plausible, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the selected block-oracle convention or its assumptions.

children.title: Sampling-Granularity Effects
children.top_down_role: Accuracy and cost consequences of coordinate versus block sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Granularity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the second-moment cost of unbiased sampling across blocks of different granularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under block sampling with fixed probabilities \(p_i>0\), define \(\widehat g=p_I^{-1}P_I g\) for a deterministic vector \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m P_i g\). Orthogonality of the blocks gives \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g]=g\) and \[\mathbb{E}\|\widehat g\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\|P_i g\|^2}{p_i}.\] Consequently, finer or more uneven sampling can enlarge the estimator second moment through small \(p_i\). Among all positive probabilities summing to one, the displayed second moment is minimized by \(p_i=\|P_i g\|/\sum_j\|P_j g\|\) for nonzero blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling fewer or unevenly selected blocks preserves unbiasedness after reweighting but inflates the second moment; norm-proportional block probabilities minimize this inflation for a fixed vector.
assumptions_latex: \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and the block projections \(P_i\) are mutually orthogonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|p_I^{-1}P_Ig\|^2=\sum_i\|P_i g\|^2/p_i\), minimized by probabilities proportional to nonzero block norms.

notation.meaning: Component of g in block i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The second-moment identity is correct for orthogonal blocks, but the minimizer statement needs qualification when some block components vanish: under the stated requirement that every probability be positive, the norm-proportional allocation generally has zero entries and only gives an infimum unless all blocks are nonzero. A supporting source is also absent.

children.title: Communication-Distorted Feedback Family
children.top_down_role: Biased or stale signals induced by distributed and communication-limited computation.

children.title: Delayed Feedback
children.top_down_role: First-order signals evaluated against stale model states.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a stochastic oracle response computed at a stale iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_t)_{t\ge0}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be iterates adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\). A delayed stochastic first-order feedback vector available at time \(t\) has the form \(Y_t=G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t)\), where the integer delay satisfies \(0\le\tau_t\le t\). It is conditionally unbiased at its evaluation point when \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-\tau_t}]=\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})\). A bounded-delay regime additionally requires a constant \(D<\infty\) such that \(\tau_t\le D\) almost surely for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed feedback is a stochastic gradient evaluated at an earlier iterate; bounded delay imposes a uniform almost-sure upper bound on staleness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y_t=G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t)\), with conditional mean \(\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})\) in the unbiased regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stale-iterate representation fits Delayed Feedback, but conditioning on the randomly indexed sigma-field \(\mathcal F_{t-\tau_t}\) requires an explicit measurability or stopping-time convention. No source establishes the intended delay and filtration model.

children.title: Compressed Feedback
children.top_down_role: First-order signals distorted by communication-efficient representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Compressed Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a standard unbiased compressor model for stochastic first-order messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A randomized map \(Q:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is an unbiased compressor with variance parameter \(\omega\ge0\) if, for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \[\mathbb{E}[Q(v)\mid v]=v,\qquad \mathbb{E}[\|Q(v)-v\|^2\mid v]\le\omega\|v\|^2.\] Compressed stochastic feedback for an oracle vector \(G(x,\xi)\) is \(Y=Q(G(x,\xi))\). If the compressor randomness is conditionally independent of the oracle noise given \(G(x,\xi)\), then oracle unbiasedness implies \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased compressor preserves each input in expectation and bounds relative compression variance; conditional independence then preserves unbiased stochastic-gradient feedback.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) satisfies the displayed unbiasedness and relative-variance inequalities for every input.
Compressor randomness is conditionally independent of oracle noise given \(G(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[Q(G(x,\xi))\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed unbiased-compressor conditions are standard and the content kind is defensible as a model condition. However, conditional unbiasedness \(\mathbb E[Q(v)\mid v]=v\) already yields the feedback mean identity by iterated expectation; the stated conditional-independence requirement is unnecessary or must be formulated through the compressor's random seed. No cited source fixes the intended convention.

children.title: Joint Communication Distortion
children.top_down_role: Combined effects when stale signals also undergo compression.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Communication Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents feedback affected simultaneously by delay and unbiased compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the message received at time \(t\) be \(Y_t=Q_t(G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t))\). Suppose \(Q_t\) is conditionally unbiased and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\|Q_t(v)-v\|^2\mid v,\mathcal F_t]\le\omega_t\|v\|^2\). Then \[Y_t=\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})+\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{orc}}+\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{cmp}},\] where \(\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{orc}}=G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t)-\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})\) and \(\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{cmp}}=Q_t(G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t))-G(x_{t-\tau_t},\xi_t)\). Under the corresponding conditional independence assumptions, both errors have zero conditional mean at the stale evaluation point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jointly distorted feedback decomposes into a gradient at a stale iterate, oracle noise, and compression noise; unbiasedness centers both noise terms conditionally.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le\tau_t\le t\) and the stale oracle is conditionally unbiased.
\(Q_t\) is conditionally unbiased with relative variance parameter \(\omega_t\).
Compression randomness is conditionally independent of oracle noise given the uncompressed message.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y_t=\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})+\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{orc}}+\varepsilon_t^{\mathrm{cmp}}\), with conditionally centered error terms.

notation.meaning: Stochastic-oracle error at the stale iterate.
Compression error in the transmitted message.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic decomposition fits the Joint Communication Distortion leaf and representation kind, but the sigma-fields relative to which the oracle and compression errors are centered are not explicitly identified. Random delay, compressor randomness, and oracle-noise measurability therefore remain unreliable without a source specifying the joint model.

children.title: Gradient Magnitude-Control Family
children.top_down_role: Magnitude-control families for suppressing extreme stochastic-gradient observations.

children.title: Global-Norm Clipping
children.top_down_role: Whole-vector clipping governed by a shared magnitude scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Norm Clipping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines whole-vector clipping at a shared Euclidean-norm threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a threshold \(c>0\), the global-norm clipping operator \(\operatorname{Clip}_c:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[\operatorname{Clip}_c(g)=g\min\left\{1,\frac{c}{\|g\|_2}\right\},\] with the multiplier defined as \(1\) when \(g=0\). Hence \(\operatorname{Clip}_c(g)=g\) when \(\|g\|_2\le c\), while vectors above the threshold are rescaled without changing direction. The output always satisfies \(\|\operatorname{Clip}_c(g)\|_2\le c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global-norm clipping leaves small vectors unchanged and radially rescales large vectors to have norm exactly the shared threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\operatorname{Clip}_c(g)\|_2\le c\), with equality for \(\|g\|_2>c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radial Euclidean clipping definition is precise, internally consistent, and appropriate for this definition leaf, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Coordinatewise Magnitude-Control Pair
children.top_down_role: Componentwise magnitude control and anisotropic truncation.

children.title: Coordinatewise Clipping
children.top_down_role: Componentwise capping of gradient magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Clipping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines componentwise saturation using possibly unequal coordinate thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For thresholds \(c_j>0\), define \(C_c:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) coordinatewise by \[(C_c(g))_j=\operatorname{sign}(g_j)\min\{|g_j|,c_j\},\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,\] with \(\operatorname{sign}(0)=0\). Each coordinate inside its interval is unchanged, whereas a coordinate exceeding its threshold is replaced by the endpoint having the same sign. Equivalently, \(C_c(g)\) is the Euclidean projection of \(g\) onto the box \(\prod_{j=1}^d[-c_j,c_j]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise clipping independently saturates each component at its threshold and equals projection onto the corresponding axis-aligned box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|(C_c(g))_j|\le c_j\) for every \(j\), and \(C_c(g)=\Pi_{\prod_j[-c_j,c_j]}(g)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise saturation formula and box-projection equivalence are correct and fit a definition of Coordinatewise Clipping, but no source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Coordinatewise Truncation
children.top_down_role: Componentwise suppression based on coordinate-level thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines hard rejection of individual coordinates whose magnitudes exceed prescribed thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For thresholds \(c_j>0\), the coordinatewise hard-truncation operator \(T_c:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is defined by \[(T_c(g))_j=g_j\mathbf{1}\{|g_j|\le c_j\},\qquad j=1,\ldots,d.\] Thus an accepted coordinate is retained exactly, while an exceeding coordinate is set to zero rather than saturated at the boundary. The output satisfies \(|(T_c(g))_j|\le c_j\), but \(T_c\) is discontinuous at every point with \(|g_j|=c_j\) under this acceptance convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise truncation retains components below their thresholds and deletes exceeding components, producing bounded output but a discontinuous hard-rejection rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T_c(g))_j=g_j\mathbf{1}\{|g_j|\le c_j\}\) and \(|(T_c(g))_j|\le c_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hard-rejection formula is internally consistent and distinct from clipping, but truncation terminology and the choice to retain equality at the threshold are convention-dependent. No citation supports this exact definition or boundary convention.

children.title: Anisotropic Threshold Selection
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-specific threshold choices reflecting uneven gradient scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Threshold Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies scale-equivariant coordinate thresholds based on predictable directional scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_{t,j}>0\) be a coordinate scale measurable with respect to the pre-feedback information \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), and let \(\lambda_t>0\) be predictable. An anisotropic threshold vector is selected by \[c_{t,j}=\lambda_t s_{t,j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,d.\] The rule is coordinate-scale equivariant: if coordinate \(j\) and its scale are both transformed by a factor \(a_j\ne0\), then its threshold transforms by \(|a_j|\), so the standardized clipping or truncation decision depends only on \(|g_{t,j}|/s_{t,j}\). Predictability prevents the current observation from choosing its own acceptance threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic thresholds multiply predictable coordinate scales by a common standardized cutoff, making magnitude control equivariant to coordinate rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_{t,j}=\lambda_t s_{t,j}\), so decisions are determined by the standardized magnitudes \(|g_{t,j}|/s_{t,j}\).

notation.meaning: Predictable scale estimate for coordinate j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predictable scale rule is mathematically coherent and its scale-equivariance claim follows under the described simultaneous rescaling. It is nevertheless one specific anisotropic threshold construction rather than a uniquely canonical condition, and no source supports its selection for this leaf.

children.title: Adaptive Clipping Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Data-dependent and time-varying clipping scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Clipping Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a predictable online rule for data-dependent global clipping thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(c_0>0\), \(\beta\in[0,1)\), \(\delta>0\), and stochastic gradients \(g_t\), initialize \(v_0=c_0^2\). At iteration \(t\), use the predictable threshold \(c_t=\sqrt{v_{t-1}+\delta}\), form \(\widetilde g_t=g_t\min\{1,c_t/\|g_t\|_2\}\), update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\), and then set \(v_t=\beta v_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\|g_t\|_2^2\). Stop according to a prescribed iteration budget and output the final iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method clips each stochastic gradient using a threshold computed from past squared norms, then updates the scale estimate after consuming the current gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_t>0\) is chosen before forming the iterate update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widetilde g_t\|_2\le c_t\), and \(c_t\) is measurable before observing \(g_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate content kind for the fully specified online procedure, and predictability follows from updating \(v_t\) after observing \(g_t\). The particular exponential-scale algorithm, initialization, regularization, and output rule are unsupported by any cited source, so it cannot be reviewed as a recognized adaptive-clipping method.

children.title: Hard-Threshold Truncation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gradient suppression policies based on hard acceptance or rejection thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Threshold Truncation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines radial hard rejection and distinguishes fixed, vanishing, and diverging threshold schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(c_t>0\), radial hard-threshold truncation maps a stochastic gradient \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) to \[\widetilde g_t=g_t\mathbf{1}\{\|g_t\|_2\le c_t\}.\] A fixed-threshold regime has \(c_t=c\); a vanishing-threshold regime has \(c_t\to0\); and a diverging-threshold regime has \(c_t\to\infty\). In every regime, \(\|\widetilde g_t\|_2\le c_t\). Unlike global-norm clipping, a rejected vector contributes zero, so the map is discontinuous at \(\|g_t\|_2=c_t\) under the displayed acceptance convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial hard truncation keeps an entire gradient only below the threshold; threshold schedules may be fixed, vanish, or diverge over time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g_t=g_t\mathbf{1}\{\|g_t\|_2\le c_t\}\) and \(\|\widetilde g_t\|_2\le c_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radial hard-truncation formula and norm bound are correct, but the three-way schedule taxonomy and equality-at-threshold convention require source support. No citation or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Clipping–Truncation Tradeoff Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Bias, robustness, and information-retention differences between magnitude-control families.

knowledge_statements.title: Clipping–Truncation Tradeoff Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares pointwise modification and bias of radial clipping and hard truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an integrable random vector and \(c>0\). Define \(C_c(G)=G\min\{1,c/\|G\|_2\}\) and \(T_c(G)=G\mathbf{1}\{\|G\|_2\le c\}\). Pointwise, \[\|C_c(G)-G\|_2=(\|G\|_2-c)_+\le \|G\|_2\mathbf{1}\{\|G\|_2>c\}=\|T_c(G)-G\|_2.\] Consequently, both outputs are norm-bounded by \(c\), and their mean distortions satisfy \(\|\mathbb{E}C_c(G)-\mathbb{E}G\|_2\le\mathbb{E}(\|G\|_2-c)_+\) and \(\|\mathbb{E}T_c(G)-\mathbb{E}G\|_2\le\mathbb{E}[\|G\|_2\mathbf{1}\{\|G\|_2>c\}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both rules bound output magnitude, but clipping makes no larger pointwise change than hard truncation and therefore admits the smaller generic mean-distortion bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|C_c(G)-G\|_2\le\|T_c(G)-G\|_2\) pointwise, with the displayed corresponding bias bounds.

notation.meaning: Radial global-norm clipping at threshold c.
Radial hard truncation at threshold c.
Positive part of a real number a.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise distortion comparison and resulting mean-distortion bounds are mathematically correct for integrable random vectors, and property is an appropriate knowledge kind for this tradeoff leaf. The record nevertheless lacks the required citation and specific locator.

children.title: Nonlinear Gradient-Transformation Family
children.top_down_role: Direction-oriented and nonlinear transformations that reduce sensitivity to raw gradient magnitude.

children.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods organized primarily around stochastic gradient direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Euclidean normalized stochastic-gradient iteration with an explicit zero-gradient convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and let \((\eta_t)_{t=0}^{T-1}\) be positive step sizes. At iteration \(t\), obtain a stochastic gradient \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\). Define \(d_t=0\) when \(g_t=0\), and \(d_t=g_t/\lVert g_t\rVert_2\) otherwise. Update \[x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t d_t.\] After \(T\) oracle calls, output \(x_T\), or an iterate selected according to a separately specified convergence criterion. Thus every nonzero stochastic gradient determines direction but not step magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each nonzero stochastic gradient by its unit direction, take the prescribed step, and return the final iterate after the fixed oracle budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2=\eta_t\) whenever \(g_t\ne0\).

notation.meaning: stochastic gradient observed at iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular normalized-SGD specification, including conditional unbiasedness, the zero-gradient convention, and the output rule. The plain statement mentions only the final iterate, whereas the LaTeX also permits a separately selected iterate.

children.title: Normalization Interpolation Family
children.top_down_role: Interpolations between raw and fully normalized feedback.

children.title: Smoothed Normalization
children.top_down_role: Normalization moderated by a smoothing scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial normalization regularized near the origin by a positive smoothing parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), define the smoothed normalization map \(S_\varepsilon:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) by \[S_\varepsilon(g)=\frac{g}{\sqrt{\lVert g\rVert_2^2+\varepsilon^2}}.\] It is defined at \(g=0\), preserves the direction of every nonzero \(g\), and satisfies \(\lVert S_\varepsilon(g)\rVert_2<1\). A smoothed-normalized stochastic-gradient step with step size \(\eta_t>0\) is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t S_\varepsilon(g_t)\). Near the origin the map is approximately linear with scale \(1/\varepsilon\); for large gradients its norm approaches one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide the gradient by a smooth positive approximation to its norm, avoiding the singularity at zero while approaching unit-direction updates for large gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\varepsilon(0)=0\) and \(0\le\lVert S_\varepsilon(g)\rVert_2<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are internally correct for the selected quadratic smoothing, and definition is an appropriate knowledge kind, but multiple smoothing conventions exist and no source identifies this one as the intended local sense.

children.title: Partial Normalization
children.top_down_role: Transformations retaining part of the original magnitude information.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-law interpolation between an untransformed gradient and its unit direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an exponent \(q\in[0,1]\), define \(P_q:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) by \(P_q(0)=0\) and
\[P_q(g)=\frac{g}{\lVert g\rVert_2^q}\qquad\text{for }g\ne0.\]
A partially normalized stochastic-gradient iteration is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tP_q(g_t)\). The endpoint \(q=0\) gives the ordinary stochastic-gradient direction \(P_0(g)=g\), while \(q=1\) gives unit normalization. For \(g\ne0\), the transformed magnitude is \(\lVert P_q(g)\rVert_2=\lVert g\rVert_2^{1-q}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise the gradient norm to a fractional power before division, continuously interpolating between ordinary gradients and unit-direction updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_0(g)=g\), \(P_1(g)=g/\lVert g\rVert_2\) for \(g\ne0\), and \(\lVert P_q(g)\rVert_2=\lVert g\rVert_2^{1-q}\).

children.title: Normalization Interpolation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Transitions between raw feedback and fully direction-oriented feedback.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Interpolation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint and scale regimes for power-law and smoothed radial normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g\ne0\), partial normalization obeys \(P_q(g)=\lVert g\rVert_2^{1-q}g/\lVert g\rVert_2\). Hence varying \(q\) from \(0\) to \(1\) changes the radial magnitude continuously from \(\lVert g\rVert_2\) to \(1\). For smoothed normalization \(S_\varepsilon(g)=g/\sqrt{\lVert g\rVert_2^2+\varepsilon^2}\), the small-gradient regime \(\lVert g\rVert_2/\varepsilon\to0\) satisfies \(S_\varepsilon(g)=g/\varepsilon+o(\lVert g\rVert_2/\varepsilon)\), whereas the large-gradient regime \(\lVert g\rVert_2/\varepsilon\to\infty\) satisfies \(S_\varepsilon(g)-g/\lVert g\rVert_2\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponent controls interpolation between magnitude-sensitive and directional updates, while smoothing makes small gradients linear and large gradients nearly normalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q=0\) is magnitude-preserving, \(q=1\) is directional, and \(\varepsilon\) separates the linear and normalized scale regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint identities and asymptotic formulas are mathematically consistent, and property fits the regime container, but the record depends on two unsourced normalization conventions.

children.title: Normalization-Clipping Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Combined directional and magnitude control for weak-moment regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization-Clipping Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A radial update combining hard magnitude clipping with smooth directional normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau>0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), step sizes \(\eta_t>0\), and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Given stochastic gradient \(g_t\), define \(c_t=0\) if \(g_t=0\), and otherwise \[c_t=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{\tau}{\lVert g_t\rVert_2}\right\}g_t.\] Form \(d_t=c_t/(\lVert c_t\rVert_2+\varepsilon)\) and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_td_t\). After \(T\) oracle calls, output \(x_T\). The clipping stage bounds the input magnitude by \(\tau\), while the second stage preserves direction and bounds the update norm strictly below \(\eta_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First clip an extreme stochastic gradient, then smoothly normalize the clipped vector, jointly limiting gradient influence and update length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert c_t\rVert_2\le\tau\) and \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2<\eta_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated composition has the claimed norm bounds and algorithm is the appropriate kind, but this particular clipping-plus-normalization construction is not canonical and has no supporting citation.

children.title: Nonlinear Gradient Transforms
children.top_down_role: Robust first-order mappings beyond direct magnitude normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Gradient Transforms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General direction-preserving radial representation of nonlinear stochastic-gradient transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction-preserving nonlinear gradient transform is a map \(T:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) determined by a radial response \(\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) through \(T(0)=0\) and \[T(g)=\psi(\lVert g\rVert_2)\frac{g}{\lVert g\rVert_2}\qquad\text{for }g\ne0.\] Consequently, \(\lVert T(g)\rVert_2=\psi(\lVert g\rVert_2)\), and \(T(g)\) is a nonnegative scalar multiple of \(g\). The associated stochastic first-order iteration is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tT(g_t)\), with output \(x_T\) after a prescribed horizon \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial nonlinear transform retains the gradient direction while replacing its magnitude by a chosen nonnegative response function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert T(g)\rVert_2=\psi(\lVert g\rVert_2)\) and \(T(g)\in\{ag:a\ge0\}\).

children.title: Magnitude-to-Direction Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior across transformations that progressively suppress raw gradient magnitude.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-to-Direction Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic conditions distinguishing magnitude-sensitive, bounded, and direction-only radial responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(g)=\psi(\lVert g\rVert_2)g/\lVert g\rVert_2\) for \(g\ne0\). The transform is asymptotically magnitude-sensitive at scale endpoint \(a\in\{0,\infty\}\) when \(\psi(r)/r\to c\in(0,\infty)\) as \(r\to a\). It is asymptotically directional when \(\psi(r)\to L\in(0,\infty)\), because transformed magnitude then becomes independent of input magnitude. It is suppressive when \(\psi(r)/r\to0\). A magnitude-to-direction transition occurs when the first condition holds as \(r\downarrow0\) and the second holds as \(r\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial transform transitions from magnitude to direction when it is locally linear for small gradients but approaches a fixed output magnitude for large gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi(r)/r\to c>0\) as \(r\downarrow0\) and \(\psi(r)\to L>0\) as \(r\to\infty\) characterize the transition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting conditions are mathematically coherent and condition fits the terminal container, but the labels magnitude-sensitive, directional, suppressive, and transition are selected terminology without a citation.

children.title: Robust Gradient Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Batch and multibatch estimators that replace ordinary gradient averaging.

children.title: Median-of-Means Gradients
children.top_down_role: Blockwise gradient averaging followed by robust central aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Median-of-Means Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise median aggregation of independent block-average stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an iterate \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), obtain \(n=kb\) stochastic gradients \(g_1(x),\ldots,g_n(x)\). Partition their indices into \(k\) disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), each of size \(b\), and compute \(\bar g_j=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}g_i(x)\). Define the aggregate \(\widehat g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) coordinatewise by \[\widehat g_\ell=\operatorname{median}\{(\bar g_1)_\ell,\ldots,(\bar g_k)_\ell\},\qquad 1\le\ell\le d.\] Use \(x^+=x-\eta\widehat g\). Ties or an even number of block means are resolved by any fixed median convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split gradient samples into blocks, average within each block, take the coordinatewise median of block means, and update using that robust aggregate.
assumptions_latex: \(n=kb\) gradient samples are available at the same iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+=x-\eta\widehat g\), where every coordinate of \(\widehat g\) is a scalar median of block averages.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent coordinatewise median-of-means gradient algorithm, but the title does not uniquely select coordinatewise rather than geometric or other multivariate aggregation, and no source resolves the variant.

children.title: Geometric-Median Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Vector-valued aggregation based on geometric centrality.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Median Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean geometric median for vector-valued gradient estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and nonnegative weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_k\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^k w_j=1\), a weighted geometric-median aggregate is any vector \[\widehat v\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^d}\sum_{j=1}^k w_j\lVert z-v_j\rVert_2.\] For equal weights, this is the ordinary geometric median. When the inputs are stochastic-gradient estimates at a common iterate, \(\widehat v\) is used as the aggregated search direction. The minimizer exists for every finite input collection, although it need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a vector minimizing the weighted sum of Euclidean distances to the input gradient estimates, then use any minimizer as the aggregate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat v\) minimizes \(z\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^k w_j\lVert z-v_j\rVert_2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted Euclidean geometric-median definition is mathematically correct and appropriately placed, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Order-Filtering Aggregator Family
children.top_down_role: Order-based and iterative filtering mechanisms for corrupted gradients.

children.title: Trimmed Aggregators
children.top_down_role: Robust aggregation based on removing extreme ordered observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Trimmed Aggregators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise symmetric trimmed mean for vector-valued gradient samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\) vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and an integer \(m\) with \(0\le m<n/2\), sort each coordinate independently: \(v_{(1)\ell}\le\cdots\le v_{(n)\ell}\). Define the symmetrically trimmed aggregate \(\widehat v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) by \[\widehat v_\ell=\frac{1}{n-2m}\sum_{i=m+1}^{n-m}v_{(i)\ell},\qquad 1\le\ell\le d.\] Thus the largest and smallest \(m\) observations in each coordinate are discarded. For gradient aggregation at iterate \(x\), use the update \(x^+=x-\eta\widehat v\) with \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each coordinate, discard the same number of largest and smallest observations and average those remaining.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta>0\) when the aggregate is used for an update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat v\) is the coordinatewise mean of the central \(n-2m\) order statistics.

notation.meaning: number trimmed from each coordinate tail
i-th order statistic in coordinate l

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise symmetric trimmed-mean algorithm is precise, but trimmed vector aggregation has multiple variants and no source establishes this coordinatewise form as the intended one.

children.title: Iterative Filtering Aggregators
children.top_down_role: Robust aggregation based on repeated detection and removal of suspicious observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Filtering Aggregators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral filtering by repeated removal of observations causing excessive empirical covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and fix a covariance threshold \(\rho>0\). Repeatedly compute \(\mu_I=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}v_i\) and \(C_I=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}(v_i-\mu_I)(v_i-\mu_I)^{\mathsf T}\). If \(\lambda_{\max}(C_I)\le\rho\), stop and output \(\mu_I\). Otherwise choose a unit top eigenvector \(u_I\) of \(C_I\), remove an index maximizing \(|u_I^{\mathsf T}(v_i-\mu_I)|\), and repeat. If \(I\) becomes empty, report failure rather than an aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly detect a high-variance direction, remove the observation most extreme in that direction, and stop when empirical covariance is below the threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On successful termination, the output \(\mu_I\) satisfies \(\lambda_{\max}(C_I)\le\rho\).

children.title: Corruption-Level Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Limits of trimming or filtering as contamination severity grows.

knowledge_statements.title: Corruption-Level Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample replacement breakdown point of a vector aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n:(\mathbb{R}^d)^n\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be an aggregation rule and let \(V=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\). For \(0\le m\le n\), let \(\mathcal{C}_m(V)\) contain all samples obtained by replacing at most \(m\) entries of \(V\) by arbitrary vectors. The replacement breakdown fraction at \(V\) is \[\varepsilon^*(A_n;V)=\frac{1}{n}\min\left\{m:\sup_{W\in\mathcal{C}_m(V)}\lVert A_n(W)-A_n(V)\rVert_2=\infty\right\},\] with the minimum defined as \(+\infty\) if the set is empty. Corruption guarantees require the contamination fraction to remain below the relevant breakdown fraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The replacement breakdown fraction is the smallest proportion of arbitrary sample replacements that can drive an aggregator arbitrarily far from its original value.
assumptions_latex: \(A_n\) maps every sample of \(n\) vectors to \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Adversarial replacements may have arbitrary magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(m/n<\varepsilon^*(A_n;V)\), replacing at most \(m\) observations cannot make the aggregate displacement unbounded.

notation.meaning: samples with at most m replacements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a recognizable sample-dependent replacement-breakdown definition and definition fits the container, but robust-statistics conventions vary and no source supports the selected displacement-based formulation or its extended-value convention.

children.title: Robust M-Estimation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Influence-controlled estimators used as gradient-oracle modules.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust M-Estimation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a bounded-score location estimator used to aggregate stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(s>0\), and let \(ho:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable. Write \(\psi=

\[
\widehat g\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{	heta\in\mathbb R^d}\sum_{i=1}^mho\!\left( rac{Z_i-	heta}{s}ight).
\]

\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\psi\!\left( rac{Z_i-\widehat g}{s}ight)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle aggregates sampled gradients by minimizing a convex bounded-score loss. Existence and measurable tie-breaking are assumed, and each observation has a bounded contribution to the estimating equation.

The displayed minimizer set is nonempty, and a measurable tie-breaking rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat g\) is a bounded-score gradient-location estimate whose individual estimating-equation contributions have norm at most \(c_\psi\).

notation.meaning: score map associated with the robust loss
uniform bound on the score norm

children.title: Robust First-Order Guarantee Families
children.top_down_role: Performance families separated by geometry, probability mode, and residual oracle bias.

children.title: Convex Heavy-Tail Objective Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Objective-performance families for convex weak-moment problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Heavy-Tail Objective Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A projected stochastic subgradient bound with explicit robust-oracle bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be closed, convex, and of diameter at most \(D\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex with minimizer \(x^*\). Suppose \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_X(x_t-\eta g_t)\), \(\mathbb E[\|g_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq G^2\), and \(\|\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-s_t\|\leq\beta\) for some \(s_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). For \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}x_t\),
\[
\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)]\leq\frac{D^2}{2\eta T}+\frac{\eta G^2}{2}+D\beta.
\]
With \(\eta=D/(G\sqrt T)\), the bound is \(DG/\sqrt T+D\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust projected subgradient descent retains the usual inverse-square-root objective rate, plus an additive floor proportional to oracle bias.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on a closed convex set of diameter at most \(D\).
The robust oracle has conditional second moment at most \(G^2\).
Its conditional bias relative to a subgradient is at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)]\leq DG/\sqrt T+D\beta\) under the displayed constant stepsize.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set
history before the oracle call at iteration t

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

children.title: Nonconvex Heavy-Tail Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity families for smooth and weakly smooth objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Heavy-Tail Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex stationarity under a mean-square accurate robust gradient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below by \(f_*\) and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Set \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta g_t\), where \(0<\eta\leq1/(4L)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|g_t-\nabla f(x_t)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq\varepsilon_g^2\). Then
\[
\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^2
\leq \frac{4(f(x_0)-f_*)}{\eta T}+3\varepsilon_g^2.
\]
Consequently, if \(R\) is uniform on \(\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\), then \(\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|^2\) obeys the same bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth nonconvex descent reaches a random iterate with small expected squared gradient, up to the robust oracle's mean-square error floor.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The robust gradient estimate has conditional mean-square error at most \(\varepsilon_g^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|^2\leq4(f(x_0)-f_*)/(\eta T)+3\varepsilon_g^2\).

notation.meaning: a finite lower bound on the objective
