children.title: Coin-Betting Potentials
children.top_down_role: Wealth and potential constructions for learning-rate-free online optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Coin-Betting Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wealth lower bounds converted into comparator-uniform online regret bounds through Fenchel conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In one-dimensional online linear optimization, let outcomes satisfy \(g_t\in[-1,1]\), initialize wealth \(W_0=\varepsilon>0\), choose predictable fractions \(\beta_t\in[-1,1]\), bet \(w_t=\beta_tW_{t-1}\), and update \(W_t=W_{t-1}+g_tw_t\). If a convex potential \(F_T:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)\) satisfies \(W_T\geq F_T(G_T)\) for every outcome sequence, where \(G_T=\sum_{t=1}^Tg_t\), then for every comparator \(u\in\mathbb R\), \[\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(u-w_t)=uG_T-(W_T-varepsilon)\leq F_T^*(u)+\varepsilon,\] where \(F_T^*(u)=\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}\{uz-F_T(z)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence-wise wealth lower bound yields a comparator-uniform regret bound equal to the Fenchel conjugate of the terminal potential plus initial wealth.
assumptions_latex: \(F_T\) is convex and lower-bounds terminal wealth as stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(u-w_t)\leq F_T^*(u)+\varepsilon\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the terminal potential

review_flags: The standard wealth-regret duality is explicit, but no coin-betting source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is suitable for the wealth–potential reduction, but no source locator supports it. The displayed identity contains the undefined literal “varepsilon” where \varepsilon is intended.

children.title: Parameter-Free FTRL-Mirror Descent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Adaptive regularization routes to comparator-adaptive online learning.

children.title: Parameter-Free FTRL
children.top_down_role: Comparator-adaptive online learning through parameter-free regularized leaders.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free FTRL
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive follow-the-regularized-leader with regularizers determined from observed gradient scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(g_t\) be the linear loss vector revealed after prediction \(x_t\), and set \(G_t=\sum_{s=1}^tg_s\). Choose \(x_1\in X\). For \(t\geq1\), construct a proper lower-semicontinuous strongly convex regularizer \(R_{t+1}\) using only \(g_1,\ldots,g_t\), then set \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{\langle G_t,x\rangle+R_{t+1}(x)\}.\] The rule is parameter-free with respect to comparator radius and horizon when neither quantity is an input and the regularizer scale is computed solely from observed gradients and a declared origin-scale convention. Output the prediction sequence \((x_t)_{t=1}^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter-free FTRL minimizes cumulative linearized loss plus an adaptively scaled regularizer without receiving the horizon or comparator radius.
assumptions_latex: Each adaptive regularizer \(R_{t+1}\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and strongly convex on \(X\).
The minimization problem has a solution at every round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is determined by past gradients without using \(T\) or a bound on comparator norm.
review_flags: Generic FTRL is standard, but a source is needed for the intended parameter-free regularizer family and regret guarantee.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the record only gives a generic adaptive FTRL template. A source must specify a parameter-free regularizer family and substantiate the claims about horizon and comparator-radius independence.

children.title: Parameter-Free Mirror Descent
children.top_down_role: Comparator-adaptive online learning through parameter-free mirror geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Mirror Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mirror descent with predictable geometry and scale selected entirely from observed gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space. At round \(t\), choose a differentiable Legendre function \(R_t\) and scale \(a_t>0\) using only \(g_1,\ldots,g_{t-1}\), predict \(x_t\in X\), observe \(g_t\), and update \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\langle g_t,x\rangle+a_tD_{R_t}(x,x_t)\right\},\qquad D_{R_t}(x,y)=R_t(x)-R_t(y)-\langle\nabla R_t(y),x-y\rangle.\] The method is parameter-free with respect to horizon and comparator radius when its rules for \(R_t\) and \(a_t\) require neither quantity, using only a declared origin-scale convention and observed gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter-free mirror descent selects its predictable geometry and scale from past gradients without taking the horizon or comparator radius as input.
assumptions_latex: Each \(R_t\) is differentiable and strictly convex on a domain containing the iterates.
The displayed proximal problem has a solution in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is a mirror-descent update whose geometry and scale use no supplied \(T\) or comparator-radius bound.

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the mirror potential

children.title: FTRL–Mirror Descent Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between the two adaptive regularization routes.

knowledge_statements.title: FTRL–Mirror Descent Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained equivalence with a differentiable Legendre regularizer and linearized losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be Legendre, let \(x_1=\arg\min_x R(x)\), and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Define \(G_t=\sum_{s=1}^t g_s\). The FTRL update \[x_{t+1}=\arg\min_x\{\langle G_t,x\rangle+R(x)\}\] and the mirror-descent update \[x_{t+1}=\arg\min_x\{\langle g_t,x\rangle+D_R(x,x_t)\}\] generate the same iterates whenever the minimizers lie in \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}R)\). Equivalently, both satisfy \(\nabla R(x_{t+1})=\nabla R(x_t)-g_t=-G_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a common Legendre regularizer and interior iterates, unconstrained FTRL and mirror descent obey the same dual recursion and therefore produce identical decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is Legendre and attains its minimum at an interior point \(x_1\).
All displayed minimizers exist and belong to \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}R)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}^{\mathrm{FTRL}}=x_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MD}}\) for every \(t\).

children.title: Scale-Free Online Methods
children.top_down_role: Online methods adaptive or invariant to rescaling of observed gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Free Online Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform positive rescaling of every observed linear loss vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online linear-optimization method \(A\) on \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is scale-free if, for every \(c>0\), every gradient sequence \(g_1,\ldots,g_T\), and every round \(t\), its decision rule satisfies \[A_t(cg_1,\ldots,cg_{t-1})=A_t(g_1,\ldots,g_{t-1}).\] Thus multiplying all observed linear losses by a common positive constant does not change the decisions. Consequently, for every comparator \(u\in K\), the corresponding regret is homogeneous: \[\operatorname{Reg}_T(u;cg_{1:T})=c\operatorname{Reg}_T(u;g_{1:T}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scale-free online method makes unchanged decisions after uniform positive rescaling of all gradients; its linear-loss regret then scales by the same factor.
assumptions_latex: Round-t decisions depend only on gradients observed before round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_t(cg_{<t})=A_t(g_{<t})\) and \(\operatorname{Reg}_T(u;cg_{1:T})=c\operatorname{Reg}_T(u;g_{1:T})\).

notation.meaning: Decision produced at round t from the preceding gradients

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scale-freeness is the standard positive-rescaling equivariance predicate for online linear optimization

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Learning-Rate Meta-Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle inequality obtained by aggregating base learners indexed by candidate learning rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{E}\subset(0,\infty)\) index online base learners with decisions \(x_t^\eta\in K\), and let a meta-method choose weights \(p_t\in\Delta(\mathcal{E})\) and output \(x_t=\sum_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}}p_t(\eta)x_t^\eta\). For convex losses \(\ell_t\), suppose the meta-regret against expert \(\eta\) is at most \(M_T(\eta)\), while that expert satisfies \(\sum_t\ell_t(x_t^\eta)-\ell_t(u)\le A(u)/\eta+\eta V_T\). Then \[\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\le\inf_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}}\left\{\frac{A(u)}{\eta}+\eta V_T+M_T(\eta)\right\}.\] A sufficiently rich grid therefore competes with the best hindsight learning rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregating learners run at different learning rates yields an oracle bound matching the best candidate rate, up to the meta-algorithm’s expert-regret overhead.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\ell_t\) is convex on the convex decision set \(K\).
The base and meta-regret bounds hold simultaneously for every \(\eta\in\mathcal{E}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\le\inf_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}}\{A(u)/\eta+\eta V_T+M_T(\eta)\}\).

notation.meaning: Meta-regret overhead relative to rate eta

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex expert aggregation plus a per-rate regret inequality directly gives the displayed oracle form

children.title: Parameter-Free Online-to-Batch Conversion
children.top_down_role: Conversion of comparator-adaptive regret into stochastic risk guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Online-to-Batch Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-risk conversion for iid convex stochastic losses and an adapted online learner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) be iid, let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[\ell(x,Z)]\), and assume \(x_t\in K\) is measurable with respect to \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{t-1}\). If \(\ell(\cdot,z)\) is convex and the online learner guarantees \[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(\ell(x_t,Z_t)-\ell(u,Z_t)\bigr)\le B_T(u,Z_{1:T})\] for every \(u\in K\), then its average \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\) satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(u)]\le T^{-1}\mathbb{E}[B_T(u,Z_{1:T})].\] Hence any comparator-adaptive regret bound transfers without selecting a learning rate or comparator radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging adapted online decisions converts their comparator-adaptive regret into an expected excess-risk bound divided by the sample size.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) are iid and the stated expectations are finite.
\(K\) is convex and \(\ell(\cdot,z)\) is convex for every \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(u)]\le \mathbb{E}[B_T(u,Z_{1:T})]/T\).

children.title: Averaged Parameter-Free Outputs

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Parameter-Free Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted averaging interface preserving the learner’s absence of tuned scale parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given online decisions \(x_t\in K\) and predictable weights \(w_t\ge0\), initialize \(S_0=0\) and \(y_0=0\). After producing \(x_t\), update \(S_t=S_{t-1}+w_t\) and, when \(S_t>0\), \[y_t=\frac{S_{t-1}}{S_t}y_{t-1}+\frac{w_t}{S_t}x_t.\] Stop at a prescribed horizon \(T\) and output \(y_T\), provided \(S_T>0\). Equivalently, \(y_T=S_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_tx_t\). Uniform averaging uses \(w_t=1\); weights chosen from observed history retain a parameter-free output interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a recursive weighted average of online decisions and return it at the stopping horizon; uniform or history-determined weights require no tuned learning rate.
assumptions_latex: Weights are nonnegative, predictable, and satisfy \(S_T>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_T=S_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_tx_t\in K\).

children.title: Comparator-Norm Adaptation

knowledge_statements.title: Comparator-Norm Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparator-dependent regret without an advance radius bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex subset of a normed space and let \(x_0\in K\) be a reference point. An online method is comparator-norm adaptive if it requires no supplied bound on \(\|u-x_0\|\) and, for every \(u\in K\), guarantees \[\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\le \Phi_T\bigl(\|u-x_0\|;g_{1:T}\bigr),\] where \(r\mapsto\Phi_T(r;g_{1:T})\) is finite for every finite \(r\) and grows with the realized comparator distance rather than a worst-case domain radius. The algorithm and its hyperparameters must be independent of the comparator \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparator-norm adaptation gives each comparator a regret bound based on its own distance from a reference point, without knowing that distance in advance.
assumptions_latex: Regret is evaluated for online linear losses generated by \(g_1,\ldots,g_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\) is controlled by the realized quantity \(\|u-x_0\|\), without a supplied comparator-radius bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: comparator adaptivity is defined by simultaneous comparator-dependent bounds without prior radius knowledge

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Diameter Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptation to an unknown finite decision-set diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded convex decision set \(K\) with diameter \(D_K=\sup_{x,y\in K}\|x-y\|\), an online method is domain-diameter adaptive if it is run without receiving \(D_K\) and satisfies a regret guarantee \[\sup_{u\in K}\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\le \Psi_T(D_K;g_{1:T}),\] comparable, up to stated universal or logarithmic factors, to the guarantee of the same method tuned with the true diameter. Any internal radius estimates may depend only on information available before the current decision; they may not use the unknown value \(D_K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain-diameter-adaptive method attains nearly the diameter-tuned regret guarantee while operating without the decision set’s diameter as an input.

Round-t parameters use only information available before the round-t decision.

children.title: Unbounded-Domain Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter-free behavior when no finite global domain scale is available.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Domain Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why diameter-dependent guarantees do not extend to unbounded feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is unbounded in the working norm, then \(D_K=\sup_{x,y\in K}\|x-y\|=+\infty\). Consequently, every regret statement whose right-hand side is monotone in \(D_K\) and diverges as \(D_K\to\infty\), such as \(D_K\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T\|g_t\|_*^2}\), is vacuous on \(K\). For example, \(K=\mathbb{R}^d\) has infinite diameter although each fixed comparator may satisfy \(\|u-x_0\|<\infty\). Meaningful guarantees in this regime must therefore be comparator-dependent, regularizer-coercive, or otherwise localized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diameter-based regret bounds become infinite on unbounded domains, even though each individual comparator can remain finitely distant from the initialization.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is unbounded in the selected norm.
The proposed bound diverges with the domain diameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_K=+\infty\), so a diameter-dependent upper bound is vacuous and must be replaced by a localized quantity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the diameter of an unbounded set is infinite, making any divergent diameter-based bound vacuous

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Scale Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regret adaptation to realized gradient magnitudes without a known Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online first-order method is gradient-scale adaptive if it requires no supplied constant \(G\ge\max_{t\le T}\|g_t\|_*\) and guarantees, for every comparator \(u\), \[\operatorname{Reg}_T(u)\le \Gamma_T\left(u,\sum_{t=1}^T\|g_t\|_*^2,\max_{t\le T}\|g_t\|_*\right),\] with finite \(\Gamma_T\) whenever the displayed realized statistics are finite. A scale-free version additionally satisfies \(x_t(cg_{<t})=x_t(g_{<t})\) for every \(c>0\), so its decisions do not encode an externally chosen gradient scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-scale adaptation replaces a prespecified gradient bound with realized gradient norms; scale-free variants also leave decisions unchanged under uniform rescaling.
assumptions_latex: Gradients belong to the dual of the decision space.
Each decision is chosen before the current gradient is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regret bound depends on realized gradient scales and does not require an input bound \(G\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adaptive online bounds conventionally replace an unknown uniform gradient bound by observed norm statistics
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Finiteness of an arbitrary envelope does not by itself characterize a meaningful adaptive regret rate; a source-backed benchmark or rate comparison is needed.

children.title: Loss-Range Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Methods operating without a supplied loss-range or Lipschitz scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Range Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptation to observed per-round loss ranges rather than a known global range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For expert losses \(\ell_t(i)\), define the observed range \(r_t=\max_i\ell_t(i)-\min_i\ell_t(i)\). A meta-algorithm is loss-range adaptive if it requires no advance upper bound on \(r_t\), is invariant under roundwise shifts \(\ell_t(i)\mapsto\ell_t(i)+b_t\), and bounds regret using realized quantities such as \(\sum_{t=1}^T r_t^2\) and \(\max_{t\le T}r_t\). Thus the guarantee remains unchanged by arbitrary common offsets and reflects the actual spread of losses rather than their absolute level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loss-range adaptation uses the observed spread among losses, needs no known range bound, and is unaffected by adding a common offset each round.
assumptions_latex: Each round has finitely many real-valued expert losses.
The learner observes the round-t loss vector after choosing its distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regret guarantee depends on realized ranges \(r_t\) and is invariant under roundwise common shifts.

notation.meaning: Range of expert losses on round t
Arbitrary common loss offset on round t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: only loss differences affect expert regret, motivating shift invariance and observed-range bounds
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition combines realized-range dependence with shift invariance in a plausible way, but an authoritative source is needed to confirm this exact convention.

children.title: Scale-Misspecification Robustness
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity when observed gradient or loss scales differ sharply from calibration scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Misspecification Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantitative robustness predicate for an incorrectly supplied gradient or loss scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_T\) be the realized scale statistic and let \(\widehat S>0\) be a supplied scale estimate. A method is robust to scale misspecification on a class of sequences if its regret satisfies \[\operatorname{Reg}_T(u;\widehat S)\le C\,B_T(u;S_T)+P_T\left(u;\frac{S_T}{\widehat S},\frac{\widehat S}{S_T}\right),\] where \(C\) is universal and the penalty \(P_T\) is finite for every positive ratio and grows at most logarithmically or polylogarithmically in the larger ratio. A guarantee that applies only when \(S_T\le\widehat S\) fails this robustness condition under underestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robustness requires misspecifying the scale to incur only a controlled ratio-dependent penalty; a guarantee that collapses under underestimation is not robust.
assumptions_latex: \(B_T(u;S_T)\) is the benchmark guarantee using the realized scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scale error changes regret only through the controlled penalty \(P_T\), rather than invalidating the guarantee.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic or polylogarithmic ratio-penalty requirement is a substantive convention that varies across method families and requires authoritative support.

children.title: Smoothness-Curvature Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Adaptation to unavailable smoothness or convexity scales.

children.title: Smoothness Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Learning-rate adaptation without a supplied smoothness scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backtracking gradient descent for an unknown Lipschitz-gradient constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) with an unknown gradient-Lipschitz constant \(L_f>0\), an initial point \(x_0\), estimate \(L_0>0\), and factor \(\gamma>1\), set \(L=L_{k-1}/\gamma\) at iteration \(k\). Set \(y=x_{k-1}-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_{k-1})\) and test \[f(y)\le f(x_{k-1})+\langle\nabla f(x_{k-1}),y-x_{k-1}\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x_{k-1}\|^2.\] If the test fails, replace \(L\) by \(\gamma L\) and repeat the trial. Accept the first successful trial, set \(x_k=y\) and \(L_k=L\), and stop according to a prescribed iteration or stationarity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking tests the smoothness upper model and increases the local estimate after each failed trial, avoiding prior knowledge of the gradient-Lipschitz constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, bounded below, and has an \(L_f\)-Lipschitz gradient for some finite but unknown \(L_f>0\).
The backtracking factor satisfies \(\gamma>1\), and the initial estimate satisfies \(L_0>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted step satisfies the quadratic upper-model inequality without requiring \(L_f\) as an input.

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

children.title: Curvature Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Adaptation to unavailable convexity or strong-convexity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observed local-curvature adaptation for stochastic first-order updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. At time \(t\), let \(g_t\) be a stochastic first-order oracle value at \(x_t\). A method is curvature-adaptive if, using only observations available through time \(t\), it constructs \(H_t\succ0\) and \(\eta_t>0\) and updates
\[x_{t+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\langle g_t,x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta_t}\lVert x-x_t\rVert_{H_t}^{2}\right\},\]
where \(H_t\) or \(\eta_t\) responds to an observable curvature surrogate, such as a gradient difference, without requiring a prescribed global curvature or smoothness bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature-adaptive method selects a positive metric and step size online, with at least one responding to observed local-curvature surrogates rather than a prescribed global curvature bound.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\succ0\) and \(\eta_t>0\) are measurable with respect to observations available through time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_t\) or \(\eta_t\) is determined online from an observable curvature surrogate without a prescribed global curvature constant.

notation.meaning: adaptive positive-definite metric at round t
positive adaptive step-size parameter at round t
quadratic form z transpose H_t z

children.title: Nonsmooth Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior as smooth structure weakens or becomes unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where local smoothness estimation must yield to nonsmooth-safe control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an update using the local secant estimate
\[\widehat L_t=\frac{\lVert g_t-g_{t-1}\rVert_*}{\lVert x_t-x_{t-1}\rVert}\]
when \(x_t\ne x_{t-1}\). In a nonsmooth transition regime, no finite uniform upper bound on \(\widehat L_t\) is implied by convexity and bounded subgradients alone: across a kink, the numerator can remain positive while the denominator tends to zero. Consequently, a rule whose admissible step is proportional only to \(1/\widehat L_t\) may collapse. A nonsmooth-safe regime must retain a positive fallback controlled by accumulated subgradient scale or another nonsmooth guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a kink, secant smoothness estimates can diverge, so a self-tuning method needs a nonsmooth-safe fallback rather than curvature control alone.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex but need not be differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity and bounded subgradients do not ensure \(\sup_t\widehat L_t<\infty\); a nonsmooth-safe fallback is therefore required.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The secant-divergence phenomenon is plausible, but the stronger claim that a positive fallback is required depends on the intended algorithm and convergence guarantee. An authoritative nonsmooth-adaptation source is needed.

children.title: Stochastic-Horizon Calibration
children.top_down_role: Adaptation to unavailable stochastic and stopping-horizon information.

children.title: Noise-Level Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Performance without a supplied stochastic noise scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Level Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online calibration to an unknown stochastic-oracle noise scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_t=\nabla f(x_t)+\xi_t\), where \(\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\). A stochastic first-order method is noise-level adaptive over a specified noise class if its iterates and output use no numerical upper bound on the conditional noise scale, while its guarantee depends on an observable or self-normalized quantity such as
\[V_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert g_t-m_t\rVert_*^2,\]
with \(m_t\) predictable. The resulting bound must specialize to smaller error when \(V_T\) is smaller, without retuning the method using an unknown variance parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise-level adaptation replaces a supplied variance bound with an observed or self-normalized fluctuation measure and improves automatically when realized noise is small.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a filtration and \(x_t,m_t\) are \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method requires no supplied noise-scale bound, and its performance is monotone in the realized scale \(V_T\).

notation.meaning: predictable reference for the oracle value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition depends on an unspecified noise class and guarantee family. A source is needed to establish which observable statistic and oracle assumptions characterize noise-level adaptation.

children.title: Horizon-Free Operation
children.top_down_role: Policies that do not require a predetermined stopping horizon.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Free Operation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime operation without advance knowledge of the stopping horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequential optimization method is horizon-free if a single infinite sequence of update maps \((\Phi_t)_{t\ge1}\) defines
\[x_{t+1}=\Phi_t(x_1,g_1,\ldots,g_t)\]
without receiving the terminal horizon \(T\) as an input, and if every finite prefix admits the claimed performance guarantee at its own stopping time. Thus, for each deterministic \(T\ge1\), the output computed from the first \(T\) observations satisfies the same stated rate family, up to explicitly declared anytime overhead, without restarting or retrospectively changing earlier iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One update sequence works for every stopping horizon; the algorithm need not know the terminal iteration count and guarantees apply to every prefix.
assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), the update map \(\Phi_t\) uses only observations available through time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(T\ge1\), the prefix through \(T\) has the stated guarantee although \(T\) was not supplied to the method.

notation.meaning: nonanticipating update map at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition blends horizon-free updates with an anytime performance requirement. A source is needed to confirm that this stronger usage and its allowable overhead match the terminal concept.

children.title: Confidence Calibration Without Prespecification
children.top_down_role: Certificate calibration when the target confidence level is not fixed in advance.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Calibration Without Prespecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reporting-time confidence selection for a stochastic optimization run whose updates do not use the confidence level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A stochastic optimization procedure has confidence calibration without prespecification if its iterates and evidence process are constructed without a user-supplied \(\delta\), and there exists a family of boundaries \(b_t(\delta)\) such that, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[\mathbb P\!\left(\forall t\ge1:\ \mathcal E_t\le b_t(\delta)\right)\ge1-\delta.\]
Here \(\mathcal E_t\) is the declared optimization error or certificate at time \(t\). A confidence level may be supplied at reporting time without rerunning or retuning the iterates, provided that the selected \(\delta\) is not chosen adaptively from the same realized data unless an additional simultaneous-calibration guarantee is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One delta-free run supports a time-uniform bound at any fixed confidence level supplied at reporting time; data-adaptive confidence selection requires a stronger guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The evidence process and iterates are constructed without using \(\delta\).
The probability statement is interpreted under the declared stochastic-oracle model.
Unless simultaneous calibration is separately established, the reporting-time value of \(\delta\) is not selected adaptively from the realized data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), \(\mathbb P(\forall t\ge1:\mathcal E_t\le b_t(\delta))\ge1-\delta\), although \(\delta\) was not supplied to the update rule.

notation.meaning: declared optimization error or certificate at time t

children.title: Parameter-Free Performance Boundary
children.top_down_role: Performance, localization, and impossibility families distinguishing formal parameter freedom from reduced tuning.

children.title: Comparator-Adaptive Regret
children.top_down_role: Online performance adapting to the unknown comparator scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparator-Adaptive Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online regret bounds scaling with the realized comparator norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In online linear optimization on a normed vector space, let \(x_t\) be chosen before observing \(g_t\), and define
\[R_T(u)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle.\]
A guarantee is comparator-adaptive if the algorithm receives no prescribed bound on \(\lVert u\rVert\), yet for every comparator \(u\) its regret is bounded by a function \(B_T(u;g_{1:T})\) whose leading dependence is through the realized comparator scale, typically \(\lVert u\rVert\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert g_t\rVert_*^2}\), with only explicitly stated logarithmic or additive overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparator-adaptive regret requires no comparator-radius input and scales afterward with the norm of whichever comparator is used for evaluation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(x_t\) is selected before \(g_t\) is observed.
Regret is measured against every fixed comparator \(u\) in the declared decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T(u)\le B_T(u;g_{1:T})\) for every \(u\), without supplying an upper bound on \(\lVert u\rVert\) to the algorithm.

notation.meaning: dual norm of the observed gradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local concept and definition role fit, but the phrase “leading dependence” and allowable overhead do not specify a certifiable regret family. A parameter-free online-learning source is required.

children.title: Scale-Sensitive Regret Family
children.top_down_role: Online performance adapting to realized gradient magnitude or variance.

children.title: Scale-Adaptive Regret
children.top_down_role: Online regret expressed through realized gradient or loss scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Adaptive Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regret adapting equivariantly to the observed loss scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For online linear losses \(\ell_t(x)=\langle g_t,x\rangle\), an algorithm is scale-adaptive if multiplying every observed gradient by any \(a>0\) leaves its decisions unchanged and multiplies its regret guarantee by \(a\). Formally, if \(x_t(g_{1:t-1})\) denotes its decision rule, then
\[x_t(ag_{1:t-1})=x_t(g_{1:t-1}),\qquad B_T(u;ag_{1:T})=aB_T(u;g_{1:T}).\]
The algorithm therefore requires no advance upper bound on \(\max_{t\le T}\lVert g_t\rVert_*\), while its bound scales with observed gradient magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling all losses rescales regret but not decisions, so the method needs no advance bound on gradient or loss magnitude.
assumptions_latex: Losses are linear and all gradients are rescaled by the same \(a>0\).
The decision rule is defined on every finite gradient history.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Exact decision invariance under common gradient rescaling is a particular scale-adaptivity convention, stronger than merely obtaining a scale-sensitive bound. A source is needed to certify this convention for the leaf.

children.title: Second-Order Regret
children.top_down_role: Online regret governed by quadratic or variance-like data quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expert regret controlled by squared excess losses rather than horizon alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In prediction with \(N\) experts, let \(p_t\) be the learner distribution, \(\ell_t\in[0,1]^N\) the loss vector, and \(r_{t,i}=\langle p_t,\ell_t\rangle-\ell_{t,i}\). A regret guarantee is second-order if, simultaneously for every expert \(i\), it has the form
\[R_{T,i}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t,i}\le C\sqrt{V_{T,i}\log N}+D\log N,\qquad V_{T,i}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t,i}^2,\]
for universal or explicitly stated constants \(C,D\), without replacing \(V_{T,i}\) by its worst-case upper bound proportional to \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order expert regret depends on the comparator-specific sum of squared excess losses, which can be much smaller than the horizon.
assumptions_latex: The guarantee holds simultaneously for all \(i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{T,i}\le C\sqrt{V_{T,i}\log N}+D\log N\) with \(V_{T,i}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t,i}^2\).

notation.meaning: instantaneous excess loss relative to expert i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed form is a standard second-order regret pattern, but its constants and logarithmic corrections are algorithm-dependent. No inspectable source supports the selected formulation.

children.title: Variance-Sensitive Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relationships among scale-sensitive, quadratic, and variance-sensitive guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Sensitive Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of realized-variation and worst-case online regret scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For expert \(i\), define \(V_{T,i}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t,i}^2\) with \(r_{t,i}\in[-1,1]\). Then \(V_{T,i}\le T\), so any valid second-order bound
\[R_{T,i}\le C\sqrt{V_{T,i}\log N}+D\log N\]
implies the worst-case estimate \(R_{T,i}\le C\sqrt{T\log N}+D\log N\). The variance-sensitive form is strictly sharper whenever \(V_{T,i}=o(T)\), because its leading term is smaller by the factor \(\sqrt{V_{T,i}/T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order bound recovers the usual horizon bound but improves it when the comparator-specific squared excess losses grow sublinearly.
assumptions_latex: A bound with leading term \(C\sqrt{V_{T,i}\log N}\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{T,i}\le T\), and \(V_{T,i}=o(T)\) yields an asymptotically smaller leading term than \(\sqrt{T\log N}\).

notation.meaning: sum of squared excess losses for expert i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison follows algebraically from the assumed second-order bound, but that nontrivial premise has no cited evidence. A source supporting the second-order context is required.

children.title: High-Probability Parameter-Free Convergence
children.top_down_role: Confidence-sensitive stochastic optimization performance.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Parameter-Free Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic convergence adapting to unknown scales with explicit failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x;\xi)]\) be convex and let \(x^*\) be a minimizer. A stochastic first-order guarantee is high-probability parameter-free if the algorithm is run without numerical upper bounds on the comparator distance, gradient scale, or noise variance, yet for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\) its output \(\bar x_T\) satisfies
\[\mathbb P\!\left(F(\bar x_T)-F(x^*)\le B_T(x^*;g_{1:T},\delta)\right)\ge1-\delta,\]
where \(B_T\) depends only on declared fixed inputs and realized, observable scale statistics, with all residual initialization or safeguard dependence displayed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With high probability, convergence scales with observed data and the chosen comparator, without requiring distance, gradient, or noise bounds as inputs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper convex and attains its minimum at \(x^*\).
The stochastic oracle obeys the noise assumptions declared for the bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(F(\bar x_T)-F(x^*)\le B_T(x^*;g_{1:T},\delta))\ge1-\delta\) without supplied scale bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: High-probability convergence depends materially on the oracle tail condition and residual initialization or safeguard terms. These are deferred rather than specified, so a particular valid theorem family cannot be certified.

children.title: Parameter-Free Impossibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failure boundaries when gradient, comparator, or domain scales are unrestricted.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Impossibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform regret is impossible when comparator and loss scales are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider one-round online linear optimization on \(X=\mathbb R\). An algorithm chooses \(x_1\), after which the adversary chooses a nonzero linear-loss coefficient \(g_1\). Regret against \(u\in\mathbb R\) is
\[R_1(u)=g_1(x_1-u).\]
For either sign of \(g_1\), choosing \(u\) arbitrarily far in the direction opposite to \(g_1\) makes \(R_1(u)\) arbitrarily large. Hence no finite bound uniform over all comparators and all nonzero loss scales can be independent of comparator scale; a valid parameter-free statement must retain comparator dependence or restrict the domain or losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even in one dimension and one round, unrestricted comparators make uniform scale-independent regret infinite; comparator dependence or scale restrictions are unavoidable.
assumptions_latex: The decision and comparator spaces are both \(\mathbb R\).
The adversary may choose any nonzero \(g_1\in\mathbb R\) after \(x_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}R_1(u)=+\infty\); therefore no finite comparator-uniform regret bound exists in this regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-round comparator-uniform counterexample is mathematically sound and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no source establishes that this elementary boundary represents the intended parameter-free impossibility regime.

children.title: Residual-Tuning Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity retained through initialization, safeguards, confidence choices, or regularization.

children.title: Initialization Scale
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity retained through initial wealth, radius, accumulator, or metric choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive seed scale underlying an adaptive guarantee of the displayed form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a normed comparator space, let \(u\in U\), let \(S_T\ge0\) be an observable cumulative scale, and let \(C,D>0\) be fixed constants. For an adaptive method whose performance bound has the form
\[B_T(u)=C\lVert u\rVert S_T\sqrt{\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lVert u\rVert S_T}{\varepsilon}\right)}+D\varepsilon,\]
an initialization scale is a fixed number \(\varepsilon>0\) selected before observations. The guarantee is residual-scale explicit when this dependence on \(\varepsilon\) is displayed. In the displayed bound, setting \(\varepsilon=0\) is inadmissible whenever \(\lVert u\rVert S_T>0\), because the logarithmic expression is then undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bound of the displayed form, a positive initialization seed keeps the expression well-defined, and its logarithmic and additive effects must be shown explicitly.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a normed space and \(u\in U\).
\(S_T\ge0\) is an observable cumulative scale statistic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed bound depends explicitly on \(\varepsilon\) and is undefined at \(\varepsilon=0\) whenever \(\lVert u\rVert S_T>0\).

notation.meaning: fixed positive constants in the displayed bound

children.title: Safeguard Parameters
children.top_down_role: Residual calibration introduced by clipping, damping, or numerical protection.

knowledge_statements.title: Safeguard Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hidden numerical safeguards in nominally parameter-free stochastic adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an adaptive stochastic method whose update uses a denominator or scale estimate \(S_t\), but replaces it by \(\widetilde S_t=\max\{S_t,\varepsilon\}\), clips a step to \([\eta_{\min},\eta_{\max}]\), or projects an estimate onto a prescribed interval. The method is genuinely free of safeguard tuning only if its guarantee holds uniformly over every admissible \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\eta_{\min}\ge 0\), and \(\eta_{\max}>0\), with no performance term depending adversely on these values. Otherwise the safeguard is a residual tuning parameter: it can prevent division by zero or instability, but the claimed parameter-free guarantee is conditional on its selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical floor, clipping threshold, or prescribed scale range remains a tuning parameter whenever validity or performance depends materially on its chosen value.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is measurable with respect to information available when the update is formed.
The safeguarded update is well-defined for every admitted parameter value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dependence of the guarantee on \(\varepsilon\), \(\eta_{\min}\), or \(\eta_{\max}\) constitutes a residual-tuning failure boundary.

notation.meaning: unsafeguarded adaptive scale at iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, but the claim is a methodological criterion requiring family-specific evidence. The clipping parameters also need the admissibility condition eta_min <= eta_max. With no citation, the asserted uniformity criterion and its applicability cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Confidence-Level Choices
children.top_down_role: User choices retained through probabilistic certificate calibration.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence-Level Choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confidence parameters that survive global learning-rate adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm return \(X_T\) with a finite-horizon certificate \(\mathbb P\{M(X_T)\le B(T,\delta)\}\ge 1-\delta\) for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\). If the update rule, clipping level, batch size, restart schedule, or stopping time must be chosen using \(\delta\), then the method is not confidence-free, even when it requires no learning-rate input. It is confidence-level adaptive only when one run, whose iterates do not depend on \(\delta\), supports simultaneous post hoc guarantees over a declared confidence range, typically through a time-uniform or confidence-sequence bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method is not fully parameter-free when its run must be configured using the desired failure probability, despite adapting its learning rate automatically.
assumptions_latex: \(M(X_T)\ge 0\) is the reported error or stationarity measure.
The probability is taken over all algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any operational dependence on \(\delta\) is residual confidence tuning unless a single run admits post hoc confidence selection.

notation.meaning: performance measure at the reported output

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the residual-tuning leaf, and the distinction between learning-rate adaptation and confidence-dependent configuration is plausible. However, the post hoc confidence criterion and its connection to time-uniform or confidence-sequence guarantees require a specific source and declared certificate model.

children.title: Regularization Residues
children.top_down_role: Dependence retained through regularization magnitude or stabilization scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Residues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization guarantees retaining bias from an auxiliary regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a self-tuning method optimizes the surrogate \(F_\lambda(x)=F(x)+\lambda R(x)\), where \(\lambda>0\) is selected externally and \(R\ge 0\). If the returned point \(X_T\) satisfies \(F_\lambda(X_T)-\inf F_\lambda\le \varepsilon_T\), then for any minimizer \(x^\star\) of \(F\), \[F(X_T)-F(x^\star)\le \varepsilon_T+\lambda R(x^\star).\] Thus the original-objective certificate retains a regularization residue unless \(\lambda\) is eliminated, driven to zero by a specified tuning-free schedule, or the comparison class guarantees \(R(x^\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing a regularized surrogate leaves an additive bias for the original objective unless the regularization vanishes or is zero at a comparator.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate suboptimality bound holds for the reported output.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Offline convex and strongly convex suboptimality interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and attain its minimum \(F^\star\) on a convex domain \(X\). An offline objective-gap output certificate consists of a reported point \(\widehat x_T\in X\) and a deterministic or random upper bound \(B_T\) such that \(F(\widehat x_T)-F^\star\le B_T\) in the declared probabilistic mode. For \(\mu\)-strongly convex \(F\) with minimizer \(x^\star\), the same certificate additionally implies \(\|\widehat x_T-x^\star\|^2\le 2B_T/\mu\). Comparisons across method families must use the same output rule, oracle budget, and probabilistic mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The output is certified by an upper bound on suboptimality; strong convexity also converts that bound into squared distance to the minimizer.
assumptions_latex: For the distance implication, \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\widehat x_T)-F^\star\le B_T\), and under strong convexity \(\|\widehat x_T-x^\star\|^2\le 2B_T/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Mapping Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite stationarity measured by a forward-backward gradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\) and \(G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}(x-x^+)\). A gradient-mapping output certificate reports \(\widehat x_T\) and a bound \(\|G_\eta(\widehat x_T)\|\le B_T\) in the declared probabilistic mode. Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\), so a zero certificate exactly characterizes composite first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate bounds the norm of the forward-backward gradient mapping, whose zeros are exactly first-order stationary points of the composite objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at the reported point.
The proximal map of \(h\) is nonempty and single-valued for \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|G_\eta(\widehat x_T)\|\le B_T\), with \(G_\eta(x)=0\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\).

children.title: Expectation Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance averaged over all stochastic-oracle and algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_T\ge 0\) be the objective-gap or stationarity measure associated with the output after \(T\) oracle calls. An expectation certificate is a deterministic bound \(b_T\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[Z_T]\le b_T\), where the expectation integrates over every stochastic-oracle sample, randomized iterate choice, and internal randomization used before output. The certificate must state whether \(Z_T\) is a norm, squared norm, function gap, or another measure. By Markov's inequality it yields \(\mathbb P\{Z_T>b_T/\delta\}\le\delta\), but this conversion generally gives a weaker confidence dependence than a direct concentration argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation certificate bounds the average output error over every source of randomness and must identify the exact error measure being averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Z_T]\le b_T\), and consequently \(\mathbb P\{Z_T>b_T/\delta\}\le\delta\) for \(\delta\in(0,1)\).

notation.meaning: failure-probability level for the Markov conversion

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon performance with an explicit failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_T\ge 0\) measure the error of the output produced with oracle budget \(T\). A high-probability certificate is a bound \(b(T,\delta)\) such that, for each declared \(\delta\in(0,1)\), \[\mathbb P\{Z_T\le b(T,\delta)\}\ge 1-\delta.\] The probability covers all stochastic-oracle and algorithmic randomness. The certificate must declare whether \(T\) and \(\delta\) were supplied before the run, whether the output rule depends on them, and whether the assertion holds only at the fixed horizon \(T\) or simultaneously over multiple horizons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability certificate bounds the output error except on an event of declared probability and records all horizon and confidence dependencies.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_T\) is measurable with respect to the randomness accumulated through output time.
The stated bound is finite for the declared \(T\) and \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{Z_T\le b(T,\delta)\}\ge 1-\delta\).

assumptions_latex: Each \(Z_t\) is nonnegative, \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, and hence adapted to \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise long-run convergence outside a null event.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the algorithm's filtration, and let \((Z_t)_{t\ge0}\) be nonnegative performance measures adapted to this filtration. An almost-sure certificate asserts that there exists an event \(\Omega_0\in\mathcal F\) with \(\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1\) such that every sample path \(\omega\in\Omega_0\) satisfies the declared limiting property. Examples include \(Z_t(\omega)\to0\) and, for a declared deterministic sequence \((a_t)_{t\ge0}\) with \(a_t\ge0\), \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}a_tZ_t(\omega)<\infty\). In particular, almost-sure convergence \(Z_t\to0\) implies convergence in probability to zero, but without an additional rate statement it supplies no finite deterministic iteration count at which a prescribed tolerance is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An almost-sure certificate guarantees a declared long-run property along every random trajectory outside one probability-zero event; almost-sure convergence to zero implies convergence in probability but does not itself give a finite iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Certificates

children.title: Asymptotic Rate Certificates
children.top_down_role: Rate descriptions applying in large-iteration regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Rate Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-run stochastic performance expressed through normalized limiting behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_t\ge0\) be a random performance measure and let \(r_t>0\) be a deterministic comparison rate with \(r_t\to0\). An asymptotic rate certificate must specify its probabilistic mode and normalization. Typical forms are \(\mathbb E[Z_t]=O(r_t)\), \(Z_t=O_{\mathbb P}(r_t)\), or \(Z_t=O(r_t)\) almost surely. These assertions are distinct: the last means that, on a probability-one event, each sample path admits finite random constants \(C(\omega)\) and \(t_0(\omega)\) for which \(Z_t(\omega)\le C(\omega)r_t\) whenever \(t\ge t_0(\omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic rate certificate compares a stochastic error with a vanishing deterministic rate and explicitly states whether the comparison is in expectation, probability, or almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_t\) is a nonnegative measurable performance measure.
\(r_t\) is deterministic, positive, and converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is one explicitly selected relation among \(\mathbb E[Z_t]=O(r_t)\), \(Z_t=O_{\mathbb P}(r_t)\), and almost-sure \(Z_t=O(r_t)\).

children.title: Limit-Point Certificates
children.top_down_role: Long-run claims concerning accumulation points or terminal behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Point Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequential stationarity certificate for stochastic first-order iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_t)_{t\geq 0}\) be random iterates in a metric space \(X\), let \(S\subseteq X\) be the solution or stationary set, and let \(r:X\to[0,\infty)\) satisfy \(r(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in S\). A limit-point certificate is an event \(E\) on which there exist indices \(t_k\uparrow\infty\) and a point \(\bar x\) such that \(x_{t_k}\to\bar x\) and \(r(x_{t_k})\to0\). If \(r\) is lower semicontinuous, then on \(E\), \(r(\bar x)=0\), hence \(\bar x\in S\). The certificate has confidence \(1-\delta\) when \(\mathbb P(E)\geq1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent subsequence whose residual vanishes certifies that its limit is stationary, provided the residual is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On \(E\), \(\bar x\in S\); if \(\mathbb P(E)\geq1-\delta\), this conclusion has confidence at least \(1-\delta\).

children.title: Anytime Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity of a stochastic certificate at every admissible data-dependent reporting time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) be a filtration, let \(\theta\) be a fixed target, and let \(C_t\) be an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable random set. The process \((C_t)_{t\geq0}\) is an anytime \((1-\delta)\)-certificate if, for every almost surely finite stopping time \(\tau\), \(\mathbb P(\theta\in C_\tau)\geq1-\delta\). Thus a stochastic optimization method may choose when to report using all observations available through \(\tau\), without fixing a deterministic horizon in advance. A simultaneous coverage guarantee \(\mathbb P(\forall t\geq0:\theta\in C_t)\geq1-\delta\) is a sufficient construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anytime certificate remains valid when the reporting time is selected adaptively from the observed optimization history.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a filtration and \(C_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
\(\tau\) ranges over almost surely finite stopping times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every admissible \(\tau\), \(\mathbb P(\theta\in C_\tau)\geq1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: certificate set available at time t

children.title: Time-Uniform Certificates
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous validity across a range of iteration indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Uniform Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous-in-time control of stochastic optimization errors or residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z_t)_{t\geq1}\) be statistics adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\), and let \((b_t(\delta))_{t\geq1}\) be nonnegative boundaries. A one-sided time-uniform \((1-\delta)\)-certificate is the assertion \[\mathbb P\!\left(\forall t\geq1:\ Z_t\leq b_t(\delta)\right)\geq1-\delta.\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb P(\exists t\geq1:Z_t>b_t(\delta))\leq\delta\). Consequently, on one event of probability at least \(1-\delta\), every iterate-indexed error, regret, or stationarity statement encoded by \(Z_t\leq b_t(\delta)\) holds simultaneously, including at any stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-uniform certificate controls the chosen statistic at all times on one high-probability event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\forall t\geq1:Z_t\leq b_t(\delta))\geq1-\delta\).

children.title: Optional-Stopping Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of certificate modes with data-dependent stopping choices.

assumptions_latex: Under every \(P\in H_0\), \((E_t,\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a nonnegative supermartingale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every almost surely finite stopping time \(\tau\), \(\sup_{P\in H_0}P(E_\tau\geq1/\delta)\leq\delta\); arbitrary possibly infinite stopping rules are covered through the crossing event.

notation.meaning: almost surely finite adaptive stopping time when \(E_\tau\) is used

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface transferring a nonnegative supermartingale certificate to adaptive stopping times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_0\) be a family of probability distributions, let \(\delta\in(0,1]\), and let \((E_t)_{t\geq0}\) be adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\). Suppose that under every \(P\in H_0\), \((E_t,\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a nonnegative supermartingale and \(\mathbb E_P[E_0]\leq1\). The optional-stopping interface is the certificate \[\sup_{P\in H_0}P\!\left(\sup_{t\geq0}E_t\geq\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\leq\delta.\] Consequently, for every stopping time \(\tau\) that is almost surely finite under every \(P\in H_0\), \[\sup_{P\in H_0}P\!\left(E_\tau\geq\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\leq\delta.\] For a possibly infinite stopping rule, validity is expressed through the crossing event rather than through an undefined value \(E_\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative test supermartingale yields a level-delta decision rule valid at every almost surely finite adaptive stopping time, while possibly infinite rules are handled by the corresponding crossing event.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call accounting for stochastic first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stochastic first-order method, let iteration \(t\) request \(b_t\) stochastic gradients \(g(x_t;\xi_{t,j})\), and let \(T\) be its termination index. Its stochastic-gradient complexity for accuracy \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\) is \[Q_{\mathrm{sg}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\left\{q:\text{the method uses at most }q\text{ gradient samples and }\mathbb P(\mathcal E(x_T)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\right\}.\] On each run, the charged resource is \(Q_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\). Function-value calls, projections, and proximal evaluations are excluded unless the accounting convention explicitly includes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic-gradient complexity is the number of sampled gradient evaluations needed to meet a stated accuracy and confidence target.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle response is a sampled first-order vector \(g(x_t;\xi_{t,j})\).
Success means \(\mathcal E(x_T)\leq\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run incurs \(Q_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\) stochastic-gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting independent data observations required by a stochastic optimization guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm observe data variables drawn from a population distribution and return \(x_T\). Its sample complexity \(N(\varepsilon,\delta)\) is the least number of distinct observations sufficient to ensure \[\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal E(x_T)\leq\varepsilon\bigr)\geq1-\delta.\] A datum reused in several iterations is counted once, whereas every fresh draw is counted once. Thus sample complexity differs from stochastic-gradient complexity whenever the method revisits stored data, forms multiple gradients from one observation, or obtains several oracle responses from a shared sample. The sampling model and the criterion \(\mathcal E\) must accompany the reported value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample complexity counts distinct observations needed for a specified optimization or statistical accuracy at a stated confidence level.
assumptions_latex: The data-generating distribution and independence convention are fixed.
Success is measured by a declared criterion \(\mathcal E(x_T)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon,\delta)\) counts distinct observations, not the total number of computations performed on them.

An inspectable source is required because sample complexity conventions vary, especially for reused observations, dependent data, and multiple computations derived from one observation.

children.title: Oracle-to-Sample Accounting
children.top_down_role: Resource comparisons when an oracle evaluation consumes one or multiple samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-to-Sample Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between stochastic-oracle calls and distinct sampled observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iterations \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(b_t\) be the number of stochastic-oracle calls and let \(U_t\) be the set of distinct data indices used at iteration \(t\). Then the oracle count and distinct-sample count are respectively \[Q_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t,\qquad N_T=\left|\bigcup_{t=0}^{T-1}U_t\right|.\] If every call uses one data item, then \(N_T\leq Q_T\). Equality holds when all calls use fresh, mutually distinct observations. With reuse, \(N_T<Q_T\) may hold; if one oracle call aggregates several fresh observations, the convention must instead charge those observations separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle calls equal samples only under one-fresh-sample-per-call; reuse or aggregation separates the two resource counts.
assumptions_latex: Each ordinary oracle call is associated with one selected data index.
\(U_t\) records distinct indices accessed at iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_T\leq Q_T\), with equality under fresh, nonreused, one-sample oracle calls.

notation.meaning: data indices used at iteration t
