children.title: Geometric Dimension Dependence
children.top_down_role: Ambient, coordinatewise, spectral, and effective-dimensional factors.

children.title: Ambient-Dimension Dependence
children.top_down_role: Resource or performance sensitivity to the full parameter dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dimension factors induced by norm conversion in first-order certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(v\in\mathbb R^d\), \[\|v\|_2\leq\|v\|_1\leq\sqrt d\,\|v\|_2,\qquad \|v\|_\infty\leq\|v\|_2\leq\sqrt d\,\|v\|_\infty.\] Consequently, converting a coordinatewise or maximum-coordinate certificate into a Euclidean one can introduce factors up to \(\sqrt d\), and converting the corresponding squared quantities can introduce factors up to \(d\). These factors are sharp: the all-ones vector attains the upper \(\ell_1\)-to-\(\ell_2\) ratio, while a one-sparse vector attains equality in the lower comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm conversion can introduce sharp square-root or linear ambient-dimension factors into first-order performance certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case norm-conversion loss is \(\sqrt d\), or \(d\) after squaring.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional norm inequalities, sharp examples, and squared dimension factors are correct, and property fits the leaf. The standard-field rationale is not an inspectable citation; a source locator is required for candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Coordinatewise Geometry
children.top_down_role: Scaling effects induced by coordinate-adaptive structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{coord}}\) lies between the total Euclidean energy scale and \(\sqrt d\) times that scale.

notation.meaning: cumulative squared gradient in coordinate i
comparison-set diameter in the maximum norm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal accumulation measure used to compare coordinate-adaptive stochastic methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given gradients \(g_1,\ldots,g_T\in\mathbb R^d\), define coordinate energies \(S_{T,i}=\sum_{t=1}^T g_{t,i}^2\) and the coordinatewise complexity measure \[\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{coord}}=\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{S_{T,i}}.\] It satisfies \[\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T\|g_t\|_2^2}\leq\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{coord}}\leq\sqrt{d\sum_{t=1}^T\|g_t\|_2^2}.\] Hence a diagonal adaptive certificate proportional to \(D_\infty\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{coord}}\) reflects the coordinates actually carrying gradient energy and is never worse than the corresponding ambient Euclidean energy by more than \(\sqrt d\), apart from diameter conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise geometry aggregates the square root of each coordinate's cumulative gradient energy and adapts to uneven coordinate activity.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Geometry

children.title: Spectral Geometry
children.top_down_role: Scaling effects induced by matrix-valued or eigenspace-sensitive metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-valued gradient geometry and its rank-sensitive scalar summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For gradients \(g_1,\ldots,g_T\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(G_T=\sum_{t=1}^T g_tg_t^{\mathsf T}\), a positive-semidefinite matrix. Its spectral complexity measure is \[\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{spec}}=\operatorname{tr}(G_T^{1/2})=\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{\lambda_i(G_T)}.\] If \(r=\operatorname{rank}(G_T)\), then \[\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(G_T)}\leq\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{spec}}\leq\sqrt{r\,\operatorname{tr}(G_T)}.\] Therefore a full-matrix adaptive certificate can depend on the occupied gradient subspace rather than directly on the ambient dimension; the upper inequality follows from applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the nonzero eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral geometry summarizes cumulative gradients through the square-root trace of their covariance matrix, yielding rank-sensitive dimension dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_T^{\mathrm{spec}}\leq\sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(G_T)\operatorname{tr}(G_T)}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary eigenvalue and Cauchy–Schwarz identities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral definition and rank-sensitive inequalities are correct for a positive-semidefinite cumulative outer-product matrix, and representation is appropriate. No source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Effective-Dimension Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence on intrinsic, rank-based, or data-adapted dimensional measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Dimension Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-dependent dimension associated with cumulative gradient spectral geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be positive semidefinite and nonzero. Its square-root effective dimension is \[d_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)=\frac{\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(G^{1/2})\bigr)^2}{\operatorname{tr}(G)}.\] Writing the positive eigenvalues as \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\), this equals \((\sum_{i=1}^r\sqrt{\lambda_i})^2/(\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i)\) and satisfies \(1\leq d_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)\leq r\leq d\). Thus \(\operatorname{tr}(G^{1/2})=\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)\operatorname{tr}(G)}\), expressing a spectral certificate exactly through total energy and a data-dependent effective dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Effective dimension converts the spectral square-root trace into total gradient energy times a data-dependent dimension between one and rank.
assumptions_latex: \(G\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is positive semidefinite and \(G\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\leq d_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)\leq\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicitly defined spectral participation ratio
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicitly named square-root effective dimension is well-defined for nonzero positive-semidefinite G, and the stated bounds and identity are correct. Definition fits the leaf. Because effective-dimension terminology varies substantially across literatures, a source is required to support this particular participation-ratio convention and name.

children.title: Robustness and Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Resource sensitivity to tails, confidence, and corruptions.

children.title: Moment Dependence
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to available tail-moment control.

assumptions_latex: The stochastic oracle is conditionally unbiased: \(\mathbb E[g(x_t;\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=m(x_t)\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditionally centered stochastic-gradient noise has uniformly bounded conditional \(p\)-th moment with scale \(\sigma_p\) whenever \(x_t\in D\).

notation.meaning: information available before sampling at iteration t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment assumption governing stochastic-gradient noise robustness comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) be a filtration, let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable, let \(g(x_t;\xi_t)\) be a stochastic-gradient oracle response, and define \(m(x_t)=\mathbb E[g(x_t;\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\). Fix \(p\in(1,2]\), a domain \(D\), a dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), and a scale \(\sigma_p\geq0\). A uniform conditional \(p\)-moment condition is \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|g(x_t;\xi_t)-m(x_t)\|_*^p\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}\right]\leq\sigma_p^p\quad\text{almost surely whenever }x_t\in D.\] The case \(p=2\) bounds the conditional second central moment. For \(p<2\), finite conditional variance is not required, so a rate or confidence certificate must state its dependence on \(p\), \(\sigma_p\), and any clipping or robust-aggregation rule it assumes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moment dependence records which conditional central moment of the stochastic-gradient noise is bounded and requires robustness guarantees to expose their dependence on its order, scale, and robustification rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment Dependence

children.title: Confidence Dependence
children.top_down_role: Resource or rate sensitivity to the requested failure probability.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterizes how a high-probability stochastic guarantee scales with failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_T\ge 0\) denote an optimization error after \(T\) oracle calls and let \(\delta\in(0,1)\). A confidence-dependent certificate with parameters \(A,B,c,\alpha,\beta>0\) is a guarantee
\[\Pr\!\left\{E_T>A T^{-\alpha}+B\left(\frac{\log(c/\delta)}{T}\right)^{\beta}\right\}\le\delta.\]
Consequently, it suffices for accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) and confidence \(1-\delta\) to take
\[T\ge \max\!\left\{(2A/\varepsilon)^{1/\alpha},\;\log(c/\delta)(2B/\varepsilon)^{1/\beta}\right\}.\]
The powers \(\alpha,\beta\) and logarithmic confidence factor form the certificate's confidence-dependence profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability certificate records both the decay with oracle calls and the extra logarithmic resource cost required to reduce the failure probability.
assumptions_latex: \(E_T\) is a nonnegative measurable error criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) satisfying the displayed maximum guarantees \(E_T\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Optimization error after T oracle calls.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the generic exponents or confidence profile. Moreover, c>0 does not ensure log(c/delta) is nonnegative; a condition such as c>=1 is needed. The plain statement also omits the explicit accuracy-to-budget conclusion.

children.title: Contamination Dependence
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to the prevalence or severity of corrupted observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Contamination Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the irreducible error contribution under Huber-contaminated stochastic feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose each oracle response has distribution \(P_{x,\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon)P_x+\epsilon Q_x\), where \(P_x\) is the nominal law, \(Q_x\) is arbitrary, and \(0\le\epsilon<1/2\). A contamination-dependent certificate has the form
\[\Pr\!\left\{E_T>R(T,\delta)+C\epsilon^{\gamma}\right\}\le\delta,\]
where \(R(T,\delta)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\), \(C>0\), and \(\gamma>0\). Thus accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is certified only when \(C\epsilon^{\gamma}<\varepsilon\) and \(T\) is large enough that \(R(T,\delta)\le\varepsilon-C\epsilon^{\gamma}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under adversarial contamination, the certificate separates sampling error from a contamination floor that cannot be removed merely by increasing the number of oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified error is at most \(R(T,\delta)+C\epsilon^\gamma\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\), leaving contamination floor \(C\epsilon^\gamma\).

notation.meaning: Arbitrary contaminating response law at query x.
Finite-sample confidence term under nominal feedback.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decomposition and exponent gamma are method- and model-dependent. The displayed upper bound alone does not establish that C epsilon^gamma is an irreducible lower-bound floor, so authoritative robust-oracle evidence is required.

children.title: Joint Robustness Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among tail assumptions, confidence requirements, and contamination levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Robustness Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines comparison and Pareto efficiency for certificates involving moments, confidence, and contamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a method \(M\), define its joint robustness profile by an upper bound \(B_M(T,\delta,
u,	heta)\) satisfying
\[\Pr\{E_T>B_M(T,\delta,\nu,\theta)\}\le\delta,\]
where \(\nu\) indexes the admissible moment class and \(\theta\) the contamination level. Method \(M_1\) robustly dominates \(M_2\) on a domain \(\mathcal D\) if \(B_{M_1}\le B_{M_2}\) throughout \(\mathcal D\) and the inequality is strict somewhere. A method is Pareto efficient in a comparison family when no other member dominates it. Comparisons must therefore retain all three coordinates rather than optimizing one after fixing the others implicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust methods should be compared by their complete moment, confidence, and contamination profiles; a method is Pareto efficient when none improves every coordinate.
assumptions_latex: All compared bounds use the same error criterion, oracle budget, and admissible parameter domain \(\mathcal D\).
Each \(B_M\) is a valid upper confidence bound for its stated moment and contamination model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nondominated profiles form the joint robustness Pareto frontier on \(\mathcal D\).

notation.meaning: Joint robustness error bound for method M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto comparison principle fits the leaf, but no source supports this particular joint moment-confidence-contamination profile or specifies the common admissible domain needed for meaningful pointwise comparison.

children.title: Adaptive-Metric Resource Costs
children.top_down_role: State-storage and metric-computation interfaces for adaptive geometry.

children.title: Memory Footprint
children.top_down_role: State-storage requirements of scalar, diagonal, block, or full-matrix adaptation.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts persistent working memory for scalar, diagonal, and dense adaptive metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an iteration in \(\mathbb R^d\) that stores the current point, one stochastic gradient, and adaptive state. Scalar adaptation stores one metric parameter, diagonal adaptation stores a vector \(v_t\in\mathbb R^d\), and a dense variable metric stores \(H_t\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\). Excluding model data and oracle-internal storage, their persistent working-memory requirements are respectively \(\Theta(d)\), \(\Theta(d)\), and \(\Theta(d^2)\) real words. If a dense symmetric matrix is packed, its metric state alone occupies \(d(d+1)/2\) words; symmetry changes the constant but not the quadratic order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar and diagonal adaptive methods use linear working memory, whereas explicitly storing a dense metric requires quadratic memory in the dimension.
assumptions_latex: The iterate and gradient are represented as dense vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\).
The full metric is stored explicitly rather than through a structured or implicit representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent storage is \(\Theta(d)\) for scalar or diagonal adaptation and \(\Theta(d^2)\) for an explicit dense metric.

children.title: Linear-Algebra Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational burden from matrix operations or metric transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebra Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares per-iteration metric application costs under common adaptive representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an update requiring \(p_t=H_t^{-1}g_t\) in dimension \(d\), a scalar metric \(H_t=h_tI\) or diagonal metric \(H_t=\operatorname{Diag}(v_t)\) permits \(p_t\) to be computed in \(\Theta(d)\) arithmetic operations. For an unstructured dense metric, multiplying by a stored inverse costs \(\Theta(d^2)\); solving a dense linear system from a fresh factorization costs \(\Theta(d^3)\), while applying an already available triangular factorization costs \(\Theta(d^2)\). These counts exclude stochastic-oracle evaluation and any exploitable sparsity, low rank, or fast transform structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying scalar or diagonal metrics costs linear time; dense metrics cost quadratic time per solve after factorization and cubic time when newly factorized.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) and the direction is computed as \(H_t^{-1}g_t\).
Dense operations use the standard arithmetic-operation model without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric-direction cost is \(\Theta(d)\) for scalar or diagonal state, \(\Theta(d^2)\) with a reusable dense factorization, and \(\Theta(d^3)\) for fresh dense factorization.

notation.meaning: Current stochastic gradient or first-order direction.

children.title: Metric-State Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage scaling associated with maintaining adaptive geometric state.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-State Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies adaptive metric state by scalar, diagonal, structured, and dense representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An adaptive metric state in \(\mathbb R^d\) may be represented as
\[H_t=h_tI,\qquad H_t=\operatorname{Diag}(v_t),\qquad H_t=D_t+U_tU_t^{\mathsf T},\qquad\text{or}\qquad H_t\in\mathbb S_{++}^d.\]
The corresponding metric-state storage is respectively \(1\), \(d\), \(d+dr\), and \(d(d+1)/2\) real words when \(D_t\) is diagonal and \(U_t\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\). Thus low-rank-plus-diagonal storage is linear in \(d\) for fixed rank \(r\), while an unrestricted explicit symmetric metric has quadratic storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive metrics can be stored as a scalar, diagonal, low-rank-plus-diagonal, or dense matrix, with progressively larger state requirements.
assumptions_latex: The metric is symmetric positive definite and stored without compression beyond the displayed representation.
For structured storage, \(D_t\) is diagonal and \(U_t\) has rank parameter \(r\le d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric-state word counts are \(1\), \(d\), \(d+dr\), and \(d(d+1)/2\) for the four displayed representations.

notation.meaning: Diagonal component of a structured metric.

children.title: Stochastic Output Selection Interface

children.title: Averaged-Output Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Averaged-output families for convex stochastic optimization.

children.title: Weighted Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaged outputs formed using nonuniform iterate weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an online weighted output from stochastic iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\) belong to a convex set \(X\) in a real vector space, and let \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\ge0\) satisfy \(W_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t>0\). The weighted-average output is
\[\bar x_T^{(w)}:=\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^T w_tx_t.\]
Convexity of \(X\) gives \(\bar x_T^{(w)}\in X\). For every convex function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), Jensen's inequality yields
\[f(\bar x_T^{(w)})\le \frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^T w_tf(x_t).\]
The weights may be deterministic or predictable with respect to the pre-iteration filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted output is the normalized nonnegative weighted sum of the iterates; convexity preserves feasibility and transfers average objective bounds to that output.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(x_t\in X\) for \(1\le t\le T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x_T^{(w)}\in X\), and convex \(f\) satisfies the displayed Jensen bound.

children.title: Tail Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaged outputs restricted to a terminal segment of the iterate sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines averaging over a terminal fraction of the stochastic trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\) in a convex set \(X\), choose a tail start \(m_T\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\) and nonnegative weights \(w_t\) with \(\sum_{t=m_T}^T w_t>0\). The tail-averaged output is
\[\bar x_{T,m_T}:=\frac{\sum_{t=m_T}^T w_tx_t}{\sum_{t=m_T}^T w_t}.\]
Uniform tail averaging uses \(w_t=1\). A fixed-fraction policy takes \(m_T=\lfloor\rho T\rfloor+1\) for \(\rho\in[0,1)\). Convexity ensures \(\bar x_{T,m_T}\in X\); the prefix \(x_1,\ldots,x_{m_T-1}\) has zero influence on the reported output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail averaging discards an initial prefix and reports a weighted average of the remaining iterates, commonly the last fixed fraction of a run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tail average is feasible and depends only on iterates indexed from \(m_T\) through \(T\).

notation.meaning: First index included in the tail.

children.title: Weighting-Schedule Effects
children.top_down_role: Certificate sensitivity to weighting profiles or averaging windows.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighting-Schedule Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how deterministic step-size weights determine a convex stochastic subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be closed and convex, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex with a minimizer \(x_*\in X\). Starting from deterministic \(x_1\in X\), consider
\[x_{t+1}=\Pi_X(x_t-\eta_tg_t),\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,\]
where the step sizes \(\eta_t>0\) are deterministic, \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\in\partial f(x_t)\), and \(\mathbb E[\lVert g_t\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le G^2\). Define
\[\bar x_T^{(\eta)}:=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_tx_t}{\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t}.\]
Then
\[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T^{(\eta)})-f(x_*)]\le\frac{\lVert x_1-x_*\rVert^2+G^2\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t^2}{2\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t}.\]
Thus the weighting schedule affects the certificate through both cumulative weight and cumulative squared weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For projected stochastic subgradient descent with deterministic step sizes, the step-size-weighted output has an expected objective-gap bound governed by total step size and total squared step size.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is closed and convex, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is convex with a minimizer \(x_*\in X\).
\(x_1\in X\) and the positive step sizes \(\eta_t\) are deterministic.
\(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\in\partial f(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert g_t\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le G^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected objective gap obeys the displayed ratio involving \(\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t\) and \(\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t^2\).

notation.meaning: Deterministic step size and averaging weight at iteration t.
Information available before sampling the iteration-t oracle response.

children.title: Last-Iterate Outputs
children.top_down_role: Terminal-iterate performance and its distinction from averaging.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates terminal-iterate performance from certificates based only on trajectory averages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A last-iterate policy reports \(x_T\). An aggregate certificate alone does not control this output: take \(X=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=x\), and a trajectory with \(x_t=0\) for \(1\le t<T\) and \(x_T=1\). Then the uniform average \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\) satisfies
\[f(\bar x_T)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\frac1T,\]
whereas
\[f(x_T)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)=1.\]
Thus a convergence bound for an averaged output cannot be relabeled as a last-iterate guarantee without additional trajectory or problem structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small averaged objective gap need not imply a small terminal gap; last-iterate performance requires a certificate that directly controls the final iterate.
assumptions_latex: The displayed trajectory is used solely to test what an aggregate certificate logically implies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(O(T^{-1})\) averaged gap can coexist with a constant last-iterate gap.

notation.meaning: Terminal iterate reported by the last-iterate policy.

children.title: Random-Iterate Selection
children.top_down_role: Randomized output selection for nonconvex stationarity guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Iterate Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomizes the reported iterate to convert weighted stationarity sums into expectation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\) and deterministic or trajectory-independent weights \(a_t\ge0\) with \(A_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T a_t>0\), draw an index \(R\) after the run according to
\[\Pr(R=t)=\frac{a_t}{A_T},\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,\]
and output \(x_R\). For every nonnegative measurable stationarity measure \(S\), conditional on the trajectory,
\[\mathbb E[S(x_R)\mid x_1,\ldots,x_T]=\frac{1}{A_T}\sum_{t=1}^T a_tS(x_t).\]
Therefore any bound \(\sum_t a_t\mathbb E[S(x_t)]\le C_T\) gives \(\mathbb E[S(x_R)]\le C_T/A_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an iterate with probability proportional to analysis weights; a weighted average stationarity bound then becomes an expected guarantee for the reported iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(a_t\ge0\), \(A_T>0\), and the selection draw is conditionally independent given the realized trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weighted-sum certificate transfers exactly to \(\mathbb E[S(x_R)]\le C_T/A_T\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative stationarity measure, such as a squared gradient norm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The randomized-selection algorithm and weighted-expectation identity are precise and fit the nonconvex output-selection leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for this nontrivial transfer certificate.

children.title: Zeroth-Order Transfer
children.top_down_role: Adaptive ideas reused with function-value or perturbation-based oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Zeroth-Order Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a smoothed gradient using symmetric function-value queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be locally integrable and define its ball smoothing by \(f_\mu(x):=\mathbb E_{v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(B_d)}[f(x+\mu v)]\), where \(\mu>0\). If \(u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{d-1})\), then
\[\nabla f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E_u\!\left[\frac{d}{2\mu}\bigl(f(x+\mu u)-f(x-\mu u)\bigr)u\right].\]
Thus a first-order stochastic update can be transferred to zeroth-order feedback by replacing its gradient estimate with the displayed two-query estimator. With unbiased noisy function values, expectation over both oracle noise and \(u\) preserves this identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric two-point function estimator is unbiased for the gradient of a ball-smoothed objective, permitting first-order updates to use zeroth-order feedback.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is locally integrable and \(f_\mu\) is differentiable at the query point.
Function-value noise is unbiased and the two queried values have finite expectations.
\(u\) is uniform on the Euclidean unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two-point estimator uses two function queries and has expectation \(\nabla f_\mu(x)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball in dimension d.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric two-point identity and representation role are plausible, but the exact regularity needed for the sphere-boundary formula and the noisy-query convention require an authoritative source. Local integrability alone can leave sphere restrictions delicate.

children.title: Bandit Feedback Transfer
children.top_down_role: Adaptive ideas reused under partial-information loss feedback.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandit Feedback Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-point bandit feedback represented as an unbiased gradient of a spherically smoothed loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(f:K+\delta\mathbb{B}_2\to\mathbb{R}\) be measurable and locally integrable, and define \(f_\delta(x)=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{B}_2)}[f(x+\delta v)]\). For \(u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\), a single bandit observation \(f(x+\delta u)\) induces the estimator \(g_\delta(x;u)=\frac{d}{\delta}f(x+\delta u)u\). At every \(x\in K\) where the smoothing identity applies, \[\mathbb{E}_u[g_\delta(x;u)]=\nabla f_\delta(x).\] Thus one-point value feedback transfers to unbiased first-order feedback for the smoothed objective, not generally for \(f\) itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized one-point function value yields an unbiased gradient estimator for the ball-smoothed objective, though generally not for the original loss.
assumptions_latex: \(K+\delta\mathbb{B}_2\) lies in the oracle domain and \(\delta>0\).
\(f\) is measurable and locally integrable on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}_u[g_\delta(x;u)]=\nabla f_\delta(x)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball and unit sphere in dimension d.

review_flags: Exact one-point smoothing identity requires an authoritative derivative-free or bandit-optimization source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and one-point smoothing identity are mathematically standard and fit Bandit Feedback Transfer, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the exact normalization and regularity conditions.

children.title: Query-Allocation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Transfer issues involving adaptive allocation of evaluations or observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Query-Allocation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-feasible allocation of zeroth-order oracle calls across iterations and perturbation directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a query budget \(Q\in\mathbb{N}\), choose an iteration count \(T\), batch sizes \(m_t\), and an estimator type requiring \(q_t\) function evaluations per sampled direction. Initialize \(x_1\in K\). For \(t=1,\ldots,T\), query the oracle at the perturbation points prescribed by the estimator, form \(\widehat g_t=m_t^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m_t}g_{t,j}\), and update \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_K(x_t-\eta_t\widehat g_t)\). The interface is budget-feasible precisely when \[\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t m_t\le Q.\] It outputs either \(x_{T+1}\) or a declared weighted average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface assigns a finite oracle budget among iterations and directions, forms batched gradient estimates, and returns a declared final or averaged iterate.
assumptions_latex: Each estimator declares its perturbation points and per-direction query cost \(q_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t m_t\le Q\), with output \(x_{T+1}\) or a specified weighted average.

notation.meaning: Total permitted number of function-value queries.
Number of sampled directions at iteration t.
Queries required per sampled direction at iteration t.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this derivative-free query-allocation formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic interface fits the leaf and its budget accounting is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the stated query-allocation formulation or output convention.

children.title: Perturbation Geometry
children.top_down_role: Interaction between adaptive metrics and randomized probing geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient representation induced by smoothing over a general convex perturbation body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be a convex body containing the origin, let \(V\sim\operatorname{Unif}(B)\), and define \(f_{\delta,B}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\delta V)]\). If \(f\) is locally integrable and the boundary of \(B\) is sufficiently regular, the divergence theorem gives \[\nabla f_{\delta,B}(x)=\frac{1}{\delta\,\operatorname{vol}(B)}\int_{\partial B}f(x+\delta u)n_B(u)\,dS(u).\] Consequently, sampling \(U\) from surface measure on \(\partial B\) yields a value-based gradient estimator after multiplication by the corresponding surface-density and outward-normal weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation body determines both the smoothed objective and a boundary-integral gradient estimator weighted by the body's outward normals.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a full-dimensional convex body containing the origin with sufficiently regular boundary.
\(f\) is locally integrable on every required translate \(x+\delta B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f_{\delta,B}(x)=(\delta\operatorname{vol}(B))^{-1}\int_{\partial B}f(x+\delta u)n_B(u)\,dS(u)\).

notation.meaning: Outward unit normal to the boundary of B at u.
Surface-area measure on the boundary of B.
Objective smoothed uniformly over the scaled body.

review_flags: Boundary regularity and sampling-density conventions need a derivative-free optimization source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary-integral representation fits Perturbation Geometry, but an authoritative source is needed to validate the boundary regularity, differentiability, and surface-sampling conventions used in this generality.

children.title: Proximal Transfer
children.top_down_role: Reuse of adaptive metrics or learning rates inside composite proximal methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-backward transfer for a smooth finite sum plus a proximable regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+r(x)\), initialize \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}r\). At iteration \(k\), obtain an estimator \(v_k\) of \(\nabla f(x_k)\), where \(f=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\), choose \(\eta_k>0\), and set \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta_k r}(x_k-\eta_k v_k),\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(z)=\arg\min_x\left\{r(x)+\frac{\|x-z\|^2}{2\eta}\right\}.\] The transferred method must preserve the estimator's sampling and state rules while replacing its unconstrained gradient step by this proximal update. It stops under a declared budget or stationarity criterion and returns the selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic smooth update transfers to a composite problem by replacing its gradient step with the proximal map of the regularizer.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and proximable.
The estimator \(v_k\) and stepsize \(\eta_k\) satisfy the source method's conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta_k r}(x_k-\eta_k v_k)\).

notation.meaning: Proximal map of the scaled regularizer.
Transferred estimator of the smooth-part gradient.

children.title: Variance-Reduced Transfer
children.top_down_role: Reuse of adaptive mechanisms inside variance-reduced stochastic methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduced Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Control-variate transfer preserving unbiasedness while reducing variance near a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose a reference point \(\widetilde x\), compute \(\widetilde\mu=
abla f(\widetilde x)\), and sample \(I\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The transferred control-variate estimator is \[v(x;I)=
abla f_I(x)-
abla f_I(\widetilde x)+\widetilde\mu.\] Conditionally on \(x\) and \(\widetilde x\), it satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_I[v(x;I)]=
abla f(x)\). If every \(f_i\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \[\mathbb{E}_I\|v(x;I)-
abla f(x)\|^2\le L^2\|x-\widetilde x\|^2.\] Hence refreshing the reference state transfers variance reduction to the finite-sum interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A snapshot control variate remains unbiased, and its variance vanishes as the current point approaches the reference point.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(I\) is sampled uniformly and independently conditional on the current and reference states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}_I[v(x;I)]=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}_I\|v(x;I)-\nabla f(x)\|^2\le L^2\|x-\widetilde x\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Full gradient at the reference point.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the finite-sum control-variate identity and variance bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The control-variate property and stated variance bound are mathematically coherent and fit Variance-Reduced Transfer, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Composite Finite-Sum Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Boundary issues where proximal structure meets finite-sum sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Finite-Sum Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle interface for a finite-sum smooth term coupled to a proximable regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A composite finite-sum interface represents \[F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+r(x)\] on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) by granting indexed access to pairs \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\), sampling access to indices, and proximal access to \(r\) through \(\operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(z)\) for requested \(\eta>0\). The interface must specify whether full sums are permitted, how many component evaluations each call costs, and whether sampled indices are independent, without replacement, or adaptively selected. An algorithm conforms to the interface only if every update and stopping rule uses these declared operations and accounts for their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface exposes component gradients, index sampling, and proximal calls, while explicitly declaring full-gradient access, sampling rules, and oracle costs.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and has a computable proximal map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i+r\) is accessed only through the declared component, sampling, full-sum, and proximal operations.

notation.meaning: Smooth component function indexed by i.

children.title: Distributed-State Placement
children.top_down_role: Placement of adaptive accumulators or metrics across workers and servers.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed-State Placement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Placement map separating replicated global variables from worker-local optimization state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For workers \(p\in\{1,\ldots,P\}\), represent algorithmic state as \(S=(x,(s_p)_{p=1}^P)\), where \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is logically global and \(s_p\in\mathcal{S}_p\) is local to worker \(p\). A placement map \(\rho\) assigns each state component either to a unique owner or to a replica set. A distributed realization is state-consistent at logical time \(k\) when all replicas required by the next update agree with the designated value \(S_k\), or when the update explicitly accepts their declared delayed versions. Moving a component across owners incurs communication; modifying a replicated component requires synchronization, versioning, or a specified consistency protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A placement map assigns global and local algorithmic state to workers and specifies how replicas, ownership changes, and delayed versions remain consistent.
assumptions_latex: The algorithmic state admits a decomposition \(S=(x,(s_p)_{p=1}^P)\).
Every update declares which state components it reads and writes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho\) determines ownership, replication, and the communication or consistency obligations for every state component.

notation.meaning: Complete logical state of the distributed method.

review_flags: Supplied distributed-optimization locators do not clearly formalize a state-placement map.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation matches Distributed-State Placement, but no cited source formalizes the placement map, replica ownership, and associated consistency obligations.

children.title: Asynchronous-State Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of adaptive state under non-synchronized execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous-State Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-state stochastic updates executed without a global iteration barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize shared state \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). At event \(k\), a worker reads a possibly inconsistent or delayed vector \(\widehat x^k\), computes an update \(g_k=G(\widehat x^k;\xi_k)\), and atomically commits designated coordinates according to \[x^{k+1}=x^k-\eta_k M_k g_k,\] where \(M_k\) is the mask of committed coordinates. The coordination interface records the read version, write mask, and commit order for each event. It requires no global barrier, but its correctness conditions must bound or otherwise model the delay between the versions used in \(\widehat x^k\) and those present at commit time. Output is a declared committed state or average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers read delayed shared state, compute stochastic updates, and atomically commit selected coordinates without waiting at a global barrier.
assumptions_latex: Each commit is atomic on the coordinates selected by \(M_k\).
Read delays are recorded and satisfy the method's declared delay model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\eta_kM_kG(\widehat x^k;\xi_k)\) defines the event-ordered asynchronous realization.

notation.meaning: Possibly delayed or inconsistent state read at event k.
Coordinate mask atomically committed at event k.
Random sample used to construct the update.

children.title: Synchronization Costs
children.top_down_role: Communication or coordination costs attributable to shared adaptive state.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path cost of barrier-synchronized distributed iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P\) workers executing \(T\) bulk-synchronous iterations. Let \(c_{t,p}\ge0\) be worker \(p\)'s local compute time in iteration \(t\), and let \(b_t\ge0\) be the communication and barrier cost after those computations. Ignoring overlap across a mandatory barrier, the wall-clock critical-path cost is \[C_{\mathrm{sync}}=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\max_{1\le p\le P}c_{t,p}+b_t\right).\] Therefore \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}\ge\sum_{t=1}^T P^{-1}\sum_{p=1}^P c_{t,p}\), and each iteration pays for its slowest worker plus synchronization. This resource bound is separate from gradient, sample, and communication-volume complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A barrier-synchronized run pays the slowest worker's compute time plus barrier communication at every iteration.
assumptions_latex: All workers must finish iteration \(t\) before any begins iteration \(t+1\).
Computation and the mandatory barrier do not overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}=\sum_{t=1}^T(\max_p c_{t,p}+b_t)\).

notation.meaning: Local computation time of worker p in iteration t.
Communication and synchronization time at iteration t.

children.title: Staleness Robustness
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of adaptive mechanisms to delayed gradients or outdated metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-delay condition controlling gradient error from stale reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let event \(k\) use a delayed iterate \(x^{k-\tau_k}\), where \(0\le\tau_k\le\tau\). If \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and updates satisfy \(x^{j+1}=x^j-\eta_j d_j\), then the stale-gradient discrepancy obeys \[\|\nabla f(x^k)-\nabla f(x^{k-\tau_k})\|\le L\sum_{j=k-\tau_k}^{k-1}\eta_j\|d_j\|.\] A transferred method is robust under this bounded-staleness model only when its convergence conditions make the accumulated right-hand side controlled, typically through stepsizes depending on \(L\) and \(\tau\), bounded update moments, or both. The delay bound alone does not imply convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With Lipschitz gradients, stale-gradient error is bounded by the intervening update lengths; convergence additionally requires stepsizes or update moments to control that sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x^k)-\nabla f(x^{k-\tau_k})\|\le L\sum_{j=k-\tau_k}^{k-1}\eta_j\|d_j\|\).

notation.meaning: Delay of the state used at event k.
Update direction committed at event j.

children.title: Compression Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Transfer issues created by compressed gradients, accumulators, or metric state.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment conditions for transferring stochastic updates through a randomized communication compressor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A randomized compression interface is a map \(Q:\mathbb{R}^d\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^d\) applied before communicating a vector \(v\). An unbiased \(\omega\)-compressor satisfies, for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \[\mathbb{E}[Q(v)]=v,\qquad \mathbb{E}\|Q(v)-v\|^2\le\omega\|v\|^2.\] A contractive \(\delta\)-compressor instead satisfies \[\mathbb{E}\|Q(v)-v\|^2\le(1-\delta)\|v\|^2,\qquad 0<\delta\le1,\] without requiring unbiasedness. A transferred convergence theorem must use the condition actually satisfied by \(Q\); these two compressor classes are not interchangeable unless an explicit correction mechanism supplies the missing property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compression interface declares either unbiased bounded relative variance or contractive mean-square error; convergence claims must use the matching condition.
assumptions_latex: Expectations are over the compressor's internal randomness conditional on its input.
The compressor parameters satisfy \(\omega\ge0\) or \(0<\delta\le1\), as applicable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface exposes either unbiasedness with relative variance \(\omega\), or mean-square contraction with factor \(1-\delta\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the stated unbiased and contractive compressor classes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two compressor conditions are clearly distinguished and fit Compression Interfaces, but no source with a specific locator supports the stated unbiased and contractive compressor classes or their parameter conventions.
